questions.stem: A patient has angioedema involving the lips, tongue, and arytenoids, with a normal trachea on CT. Which region of the airway is affected?
options: The lower airway: trachea and mainstem bronchi
The mouth, larynx, trachea, and bronchioles
The pharynx, larynx, trachea, and carina below the cords
questions.explanation: The upper airway includes the nose, mouth, pharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, and cricoid cartilage; the lower airway starts at the trachea.

questions.stem: A CT shows a mass narrowing the left mainstem bronchus 3 cm below the carina. Which part of the airway is involved?
options: The upper airway, which includes the larynx and pharynx
questions.explanation: The lower airway begins at the trachea and includes the bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli.

questions.stem: An infant has micrognathia and a cleft palate from abnormal first-arch development. Which embryologic structures give rise to the airway?
questions.explanation: Airway structures derive from pharyngeal arches 1–4 and 6; first-arch problems affect the mandible and palate.

questions.stem: A patient breathing through a tracheostomy loses the normal functions of the nose. Which functions are bypassed? (Select 2)
options: Warming of the trachea from the outside
questions.explanation: The nose humidifies, filters, and adds resistance to airflow. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, and phonation at the larynx.

questions.stem: Before a nasal intubation, you topicalize the nasal mucosa. Which nerves carry sensation from the nose?
questions.explanation: Nasal sensation comes from the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) branches of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.stem: A nasal intubation causes brisk epistaxis. Which arteries supply the nasal mucosa?
questions.explanation: The nose is supplied by branches of the maxillary, ophthalmic, and facial arteries; vasoconstrictors reduce bleeding.

questions.stem: Loss of upper-airway muscle tone during anesthesia produces obstruction behind the tongue. Which additional structure commonly contributes to the same collapsible segment?
questions.explanation: Relaxation of the tongue and soft palate can obstruct the airway.

questions.stem: A pediatric anesthesia team is preparing for several children with known airway problems. Which congenital conditions predispose to airway obstruction? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Pierre Robin (micrognathia, glossoptosis) and Down syndrome (macroglossia, small airway) predispose to obstruction.

questions.stem: During a Mallampati exam, you see the soft palate rise as the patient breathes. Which statement about the palate is correct?
options: The hard palate is posterior and mobile
The soft palate is anterior and fixed
questions.explanation: The hard palate is the fixed anterior two-thirds; the soft palate is the mobile posterior third.

questions.stem: On an airway exam, you see the arches leading from the mouth into the throat, with the tonsils between them. What is this opening?
questions.explanation: The fauces is the opening from the oral cavity into the oropharynx.

questions.stem: On a Mallampati exam, you see the soft palate, uvula, and fauces. Why does the fauces matter?
options: It distinguishes Mallampati class I and II from class III
It predicts difficult mask ventilation alone
questions.explanation: Seeing the fauces is part of the Mallampati classification, distinguishing lower classes from class III and IV.

questions.stem: A patient has a hypopharyngeal tumor seen on CT at about the level of C5–C6. Which pharyngeal segment is involved?
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx sits at C1, the oropharynx at C2–C3, and the hypopharynx at C5–C6.

questions.stem: A patient with a deep propofol anesthetic regurgitates gastric contents into the pharynx. Which structure normally prevents this?
questions.explanation: The upper esophageal sphincter prevents regurgitation into the pharynx, and anesthetics relax it.

questions.stem: During an awake fiberoptic intubation, the patient coughs as the scope touches the epiglottis despite a glossopharyngeal block. Which nerve was not blocked?
questions.explanation: The internal SLN provides sensation above the cords, including the epiglottis; it needs its own block or topicalization.

questions.stem: Which nerve provides motor innervation to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The RLN is motor to the larynx except the cricothyroid.

questions.stem: After neck surgery, a patient cannot tense the vocal cord effectively but has preserved recurrent-laryngeal motor function. Which muscle is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid is the exception, supplied by the external SLN.

questions.stem: After a thyroidectomy, a patient has a weak, breathy voice and coughs when drinking water. What is the MOST likely injury?
questions.explanation: Unilateral RLN injury causes hoarseness and aspiration; bilateral injury can cause respiratory distress.

questions.stem: After a total thyroidectomy, a patient develops stridor and severe respiratory distress immediately after extubation. Her cords sit near midline and do not move. What is happening?
options: Superior laryngeal nerve injury with voice fatigue
Bilateral RLN injury with both cords near midline
Unilateral RLN injury with normal breathing
questions.explanation: Bilateral RLN injury leaves both cords near midline, obstructing the airway, and often requires reintubation.

questions.stem: Which two cranial nerves provide the major motor and sensory innervation of the pharynx and larynx? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves supply the pharynx and larynx. The phrenic, facial, trigeminal, and hypoglossal nerves do not.

questions.stem: On a neck CT, the larynx spans from the hyoid level down to the cricoid. Between which vertebral levels does it extend?
questions.explanation: The larynx extends from about C3 to C6.

questions.stem: A trauma patient has fractures of the thyroid cartilage, the cricoid, and the epiglottis. Which group of cartilages are these?
questions.explanation: The thyroid, cricoid, and epiglottis are the three single (unpaired) laryngeal cartilages.

questions.stem: After traumatic intubation, an arytenoid is dislocated. Which classification correctly places this cartilage?
questions.explanation: The arytenoid, corniculate, and cuneiform cartilages are paired.

questions.stem: Which are functions of the larynx? (Select 2)
options: Protects the lower airway from aspiration
questions.explanation: The larynx protects the lower airway from aspiration and enables gag and cough reflexes, along with phonation and patency.

questions.stem: During a CICO emergency, you palpate a soft depression between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages. What is this structure?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane connects the thyroid and cricoid cartilages and is the site for emergency cricothyrotomy.

questions.stem: To find the cricothyroid membrane, you first locate the "Adam's apple." Where does the thyroid cartilage fuse anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The thyroid cartilage laminae fuse anteriorly at the thyroid notch.

questions.stem: Bleeding from the supraglottic larynx is traced to a branch of the superior thyroid artery. Which vessel is involved?
questions.explanation: The superior laryngeal artery, from the superior thyroid artery, supplies the supraglottic larynx.

questions.stem: Bleeding from the infraglottic larynx is traced to a branch of the inferior thyroid artery. Which vessel is involved?
questions.explanation: The inferior laryngeal artery, from the inferior thyroid artery, supplies the infraglottic larynx.

questions.stem: After a laryngeal nerve injury, a patient cannot fully close his glottis or tense his cords. Which muscles control these functions?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles control cord tension and glottic opening and closure.

questions.stem: A patient after neck surgery has trouble elevating his larynx when swallowing. Which muscles position the larynx during swallowing and breathing?
questions.explanation: Extrinsic laryngeal muscles position the larynx during phonation, breathing, and swallowing.

questions.stem: During DL, you see a small pocket between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis. What is it?
questions.explanation: The vallecula lies between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis.

questions.stem: You use a Macintosh 3 blade and need to lift the epiglottis indirectly. Where should the tip be placed?
questions.explanation: The Mac blade tip sits in the vallecula and lifts the epiglottis via the hyoepiglottic ligament.

questions.stem: An ETT tip sits 1 cm below the cricoid ring. Which part of the airway has it entered?
questions.explanation: The trachea begins at the cricoid cartilage and ends at the carina.

questions.stem: An adult's ETT is advanced through the cords. About how long is the trachea it travels down?
questions.explanation: The adult trachea is about 10–20 cm long, so a tube can easily be advanced too far.

questions.stem: On a bronchoscopy, you count the tracheal rings. About how many C-shaped rings should there be?
questions.explanation: The trachea contains 16–20 C-shaped cartilage rings.

questions.stem: An ETT cuff causes pressure injury at the narrowest complete ring in the airway. Which cartilage is this?
questions.explanation: The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring in the airway.

questions.stem: When a patient coughs, the posterior tracheal wall narrows the lumen. Which structure does this, and what else does it allow?
options: The trachealis muscle, which also allows esophageal expansion
The cricoid, which prevents esophageal reflux
The thyroid cartilage, which closes the glottis
The cricothyroid membrane, which controls tension
questions.explanation: The trachealis muscle aids cough and lets the esophagus expand during swallowing.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma has bronchoconstriction in the smallest airways, which lack cartilage. At what diameter does cartilage disappear?
options: About 5 mm, at the segmental bronchi
About 1 cm, at the mainstem bronchi
questions.explanation: Cartilage disappears at about 0.6–0.8 mm, so bronchiolar patency depends on smooth muscle tone.

questions.stem: An ETT is advanced too far and enters a mainstem bronchus. Which mainstem bronchus has a steeper angle from the trachea?
questions.explanation: The right mainstem leaves the trachea at about 25–30°, making it more in line with the trachea than the left.

questions.stem: After intubation, breath sounds are absent on the left. Why does endobronchial intubation usually go right?
options: The right is steeper and straighter
questions.explanation: The right mainstem is wider, shorter, and more vertical, so a deep tube tends to enter it.

questions.stem: A patient intubated with a right-sided double-lumen tube develops right upper lobe collapse. Why is the right upper lobe vulnerable?
options: Its bronchus takes off about 2.5 cm below the carina
Its bronchus takes off 10 cm below the carina
Its bronchus is narrower than the left upper lobe bronchus
It arises from the left mainstem
questions.explanation: The right upper lobe bronchus arises about 2.5 cm from the carina, so a deep cuff can occlude it.

questions.stem: A patient develops bronchoconstriction from vagal stimulation during airway manipulation. Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the trachea?
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the trachea and bronchi.

questions.stem: After intubation, the ETT is advanced too far and the patient coughs violently with a spike in BP and HR. Which structure is MOST likely being stimulated?
options: The epiglottis in the upper airway
The carina, which is highly sensitive
The vocal cords, which are insensitive under GA
questions.explanation: The carina is highly sensitive; contact causes coughing, bronchospasm, and hemodynamic responses.

questions.stem: During which embryonic stage does the lung bud form?
questions.explanation: The laryngotracheal groove and lung bud form in the embryonic stage.

questions.stem: A fetal lung development lecture covers branching of the airway into its segments. By what point do bronchopulmonary segments appear?
questions.explanation: Bronchopulmonary segments appear by day 42 of gestation.

questions.stem: A 25-week preterm infant needs surfactant therapy. During which stage does surfactant production begin?
questions.explanation: Surfactant production begins in the canalicular stage (weeks 16–26).

questions.stem: A 24-week infant has severe respiratory failure. Why is gas exchange so limited at this age?
options: Alveoli are fully mature at 24 weeks
questions.explanation: The blood-gas barrier begins forming around week 26, so earlier infants have limited gas exchange.

questions.stem: A parent asks when postnatal alveolar development is essentially complete enough to approach the adult pattern. Which answer best matches the lecture?
questions.explanation: Alveolar development continues until about 3 years of age and beyond with growth.

questions.stem: During which stage does rapid branching (≥16 generations) and terminal bronchiole formation occur?
questions.explanation: The pseudoglandular stage (weeks 6–16) features rapid branching.

questions.stem: After an interscalene block, a patient has dyspnea and an elevated hemidiaphragm. Which nerve was affected, and what are its roots?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) innervates the diaphragm and is often blocked by interscalene injections.

questions.stem: Which two embryologic structures make major contributions to diaphragm development? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum and pleuroperitoneal folds, along with the dorsal esophageal mesentery and body wall.

questions.stem: A newborn has a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the chest. What abnormal development causes this?
questions.explanation: Abnormal diaphragm development leads to congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

questions.stem: The lining of the lower respiratory tract and its supporting tissues form from which germ layers?
questions.explanation: The lower respiratory tract develops from endodermal epithelium and surrounding mesoderm.

questions.stem: A developmental biology question asks which growth factors drive branching of the fetal lung and its vascular network. Which pair is correct?
questions.explanation: FGF-10 drives airway branching and VEGF drives pulmonary vascular development.

questions.stem: During swallowing, which structure helps protect the glottic opening from entering material?
questions.explanation: The epiglottis covers the glottis during swallowing.

questions.stem: During DL, you see folds running from the epiglottis to the arytenoids on each side of the laryngeal inlet. What are they?
questions.explanation: The aryepiglottic folds lie lateral to the laryngeal inlet.

questions.stem: What lies lateral to the aryepiglottic folds where foreign bodies often lodge?
questions.explanation: The piriform recesses lie lateral to the aryepiglottic folds.

questions.stem: After a thyroidectomy, a singer cannot reach high notes, though her voice is otherwise normal. Which muscle is likely affected?
options: The posterior cricoarytenoid, which abducts the cords
The lateral cricoarytenoid, which adducts the cords
The thyroarytenoid, which relaxes the cords
The cricothyroid, which tenses the cords
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid (external SLN) tenses the cords; injury causes loss of high pitch.

questions.stem: After bilateral nerve injury, a patient's cords cannot open. Which muscle is the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor; losing it bilaterally causes obstruction.

questions.stem: During emergence, a patient develops laryngospasm with tightly closed cords. Which muscles produce this adduction?
questions.explanation: The thyroarytenoid and lateral cricoarytenoid (RLN) adduct the cords; the cricothyroid (SLN) tenses them. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor.

questions.stem: You examine a patient with a short neck and limited mouth opening before an elective thyroidectomy. What is the main purpose of this evaluation?
options: Identifying challenges and forming a patient-specific airway plan
Predicting every difficult airway with certainty
Replacing the need for backup equipment
Determining the surgeon's positioning plan for the case
questions.explanation: Airway evaluation identifies potential challenges so you can build a specific plan with backups.

questions.stem: A patient has a Mallampati I score but a thyromental distance of 4 cm and limited neck extension. How should you interpret these findings?
options: Trust the Mallampati score, which is the reliable test
Rely on the neck extension finding alone
Combine them, since no single test reliably predicts difficulty
questions.explanation: Individual airway tests have low sensitivity and specificity, so findings must be combined.

questions.stem: Which four airway management areas should be assessed? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The four areas are BMV, DL/VL with TI, SGA placement, and cricothyrotomy.

questions.stem: Which historical clues suggest prior airway difficulty? (Select 2)
options: Chipped teeth after a prior anesthetic
questions.explanation: Clues to prior airway difficulty include chipped teeth and unexpected ICU admission, as well as sore throat and remembered difficult intubation.

questions.stem: Your department performs 5,000 intubations a year. How many would you expect to be difficult?
questions.explanation: Difficult tracheal intubation occurs in about 1.5–8.5% of cases.

questions.stem: Of those same 5,000 intubations, how many would you expect to fail outright?
questions.explanation: Failed tracheal intubation occurs in about 0.3–0.5% of cases, varying by setting.

questions.stem: A student examines a supine patient who says "ahh" during the Mallampati exam. What should be changed to perform the modified exam correctly?
options: Have the patient phonate with the head flexed
Examine with the mouth half open
Seat the patient upright, tongue out, without phonation
Keep the patient supine with phonation
questions.explanation: The modified Mallampati is done seated upright, mouth open, tongue protruded, without phonation.

questions.stem: On exam, you see the soft palate, the entire uvula, the fauces, and the tonsillar pillars. Which Mallampati class is this?
questions.explanation: Class I shows the soft palate, uvula, fauces, and pillars or tonsils.

questions.stem: On exam, you see the soft palate and only the base of the uvula. Which class is this, and what does it predict?
options: Class IV, with no visible soft palate
questions.explanation: Class III shows the soft palate and base of the uvula and is associated with difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: On exam, you see only the hard palate; the soft palate is hidden by the tongue. Which class is this?
questions.explanation: Class IV shows only the hard palate.

questions.stem: Four patients have Mallampati classes I, II, III, and IV. Which patients have increased risk of difficult laryngoscopy?
questions.explanation: Mallampati classes III and IV predict increased difficulty.

questions.stem: On a Mallampati exam, you can see the tip of the epiglottis above the tongue. What is this finding, and how common is it?
options: A sign of a difficult airway in most cases
Class zero, seen in about 1.2% of patients
Class I, seen in most patients
questions.explanation: Mallampati class zero means the epiglottis is visible, found in about 1.2% of patients.

questions.stem: A patient's Mallampati exam is done while saying "ah." What is the problem?
options: Phonation can falsely improve the view
questions.explanation: The test is done without phonation.

questions.stem: Which tests should be combined with Mallampati to improve prediction? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Combine MMC with TMD, interincisor gap, and neck circumference.

questions.stem: After intubation, you document "grade 2a." What does this grading system describe?
options: The oropharyngeal view on preop exam
questions.explanation: The Cormack-Lehane system grades the laryngoscopic view.

questions.stem: On DL, you see the entire glottic opening, including the anterior commissure. What is the CL grade?
questions.explanation: Grade I is a full view of the glottis including the anterior commissure.

questions.stem: On DL, you see the posterior half of the cords plus the arytenoids. What is the CL grade?
questions.explanation: Grade IIa shows a partial view of the cords with the posterior cartilages.

questions.stem: On direct laryngoscopy, you see the epiglottis but no part of the glottic opening. What is the Cormack-Lehane grade?
questions.explanation: Grade III shows the epiglottis only, with no glottis. Grade IV shows neither epiglottis nor glottis.

questions.stem: On DL, you see only the soft palate, with no epiglottis or glottis. What is the CL grade?
questions.explanation: Grade IV shows neither the epiglottis nor the glottis.

questions.stem: Of CL grades I, IIa, IIb, III, and IV, which are generally easier intubations?
questions.explanation: Grades I and IIa are generally easier; grade IIb and higher are associated with difficulty.

questions.stem: You perform DL on a typical adult and see about half of the vocal cords. Which grade is this, and how common is it?
options: Grade II, the most common view
Grade I, the most common view
Grade III, the most common view
questions.explanation: Grade II, seeing part of the cords, is the most common view.

questions.stem: On DL, you see no laryngeal structures at all, not even the epiglottis. What is the BEST next step?
options: Proceed blindly with a Mac blade
Apply cricoid pressure and try again unchanged
Pass a bougie through the visible cords
questions.explanation: A grade IV view means nothing is visible. Reposition, readjust, or move to VL rather than repeating the same attempt.

questions.stem: A student measures TMD with the patient's head flexed and mouth open. How should it be measured?
options: Sternal notch to mentum, mouth closed
Thyroid notch to mentum, head extended, mouth closed
Thyroid notch to mentum, head flexed, mouth open
questions.explanation: TMD is measured from the thyroid notch to the mentum with the head extended and mouth closed.

questions.stem: A patient's TMD is 2 fingerbreadths (about 4 cm). How does this compare with normal?
options: It is normal; TMD does not matter
It is normal; normal is at least 4 cm
It is long; normal is under 3 cm
questions.explanation: A normal TMD is at least 6 cm; a short TMD predicts a poor view.

questions.stem: A thyromental distance of 10 cm should raise concern for which anatomic problem during direct laryngoscopy?
questions.explanation: A TMD over 9 cm may indicate a caudally placed larynx that is hard to visualize.

questions.stem: A patient with a receding chin has a TMD of 4 cm. Why is laryngoscopy likely to be difficult?
options: The cords are too far posterior
The larynx sits too low in the neck
No room to displace the tongue
questions.explanation: A small mandibular space prevents tongue displacement, blocking the glottic view.

questions.stem: Which conditions are associated with abnormal TMD? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Abnormal TMD is associated with mandibular hypoplasia and OSA, and a short TMD suggests an anterior larynx.

questions.stem: During a 3-3-2 assessment, which three distances are measured?
options: Mouth opening, neck extension, and Mallampati
Interincisor gap, mentum to hyoid, and hyoid to thyroid
Mentum to sternum, thyroid to cricoid, and nose to chin
questions.explanation: The 3-3-2 rule measures mouth opening, mentum to hyoid, and hyoid to thyroid notch.

questions.stem: What does fewer than 2 fingerbreadths between the hyoid and thyroid notch suggest?
options: An anterior larynx that is harder to visualize
A low larynx with a deep visual field
Normal laryngeal position for most adults
questions.explanation: Less than 2 fingerbreadths suggests an anterior larynx.

questions.stem: What does more than 2 fingerbreadths between the mandible-neck junction and thyroid notch suggest?
options: An anterior larynx that is harder to visualize
A low larynx that is deeper and harder to see
questions.explanation: More than 2 suggests a low larynx.

questions.stem: A patient with TMJ disease opens her mouth 2.5 cm. What does this predict?
options: Difficult mask ventilation but easy intubation
Difficult intubation, since the gap is under 3 cm
An easy intubation, since 2.5 cm is adequate
questions.explanation: An interincisor gap under 3 cm predicts difficult intubation.

questions.stem: A patient's mouth opening is 2 fingerbreadths. Why does this make laryngoscopy hard?
options: The tongue falls back and obstructs the view
The blade and tube cannot pass
questions.explanation: Limited mouth opening prevents the blade and tube from passing.

questions.stem: Large protruding upper incisors most directly worsen direct laryngoscopy by increasing which paired risks?
options: Dental injury and a less favorable line of sight
Easier laryngoscopy and less dental trauma
Reduced aspiration risk and easier tube passage
questions.explanation: Prominent upper incisors increase dental injury risk and narrow the line of sight.

questions.stem: A student measures SMD with the mouth open and head flexed. How should it be measured?
options: Thyroid notch to mentum, mouth open
Sternal notch to hyoid, head flexed
questions.explanation: SMD is measured from the sternal notch to the mentum with the head extended and mouth closed.

questions.stem: A patient's SMD with full extension is 11 cm. What does this predict?
options: Nothing, since SMD is not predictive
Difficult laryngoscopy, since SMD is under 12.5 cm
questions.explanation: An SMD under 12.5 cm is associated with difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient's SMD is 13 cm in neutral and 16 cm in full extension. Does the change suggest difficulty?
options: Yes, if the SMD exceeds 20 cm
Yes; a change under 5 cm suggests difficulty
No; a 3 cm change is normal
No; SMD change is not predictive
questions.explanation: A change of less than 5 cm from neutral to extension suggests difficult laryngoscopy; this patient changed only 3 cm.

questions.stem: A healthy patient extends his head at the atlantooccipital joint. About how much extension is normal?
questions.explanation: The AO joint normally allows up to 35° of extension.

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis can extend the AO joint only 18°. What does this predict?
questions.explanation: Less than 23° of AO extension predicts difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: By how much does neck flexion/extension decrease from age 16 to 75?
questions.explanation: Range of motion decreases about 20% with age.

questions.stem: Which conditions reduce atlantooccipital mobility? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Degenerative cervical disease and cervical trauma limit atlantooccipital mobility, as does Down syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient in a halo fixator has no cervical mobility. Which approaches are effective?
options: A Miller blade with neck flexion
questions.explanation: When cervical mobility is limited, VL or flexible endoscopy avoids the need for neck extension.

questions.stem: A patient tries to bite his upper lip with his lower incisors. What does this test assess?
questions.explanation: The upper lip bite test assesses mandibular protrusion and TMJ mobility.

questions.stem: A patient cannot reach his upper lip with his lower incisors at all. Which ULBT class is this, and what does it suggest?
options: Class B, suggesting an easy airway
Class C, suggesting easy mask ventilation
Class A, suggesting an easy airway
questions.explanation: ULBT class C (cannot bite the upper lip) suggests difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient bites well above the upper lip's vermilion border, covering it fully. Which ULBT class is this?
questions.explanation: Class A means the lower incisors bite above the vermilion border.

questions.stem: An edentulous patient attempts the upper lip bite test. Why is the result less reliable?
options: The test depends on lower incisors
questions.explanation: The ULBT relies on lower incisors, so it is less reliable in edentulous patients or when used alone.

questions.stem: A patient's neck circumference is 46 cm. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: A neck circumference over 43 cm suggests airway difficulty.

questions.stem: Which exam findings suggest difficult laryngoscopy? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: A prominent overbite and a high, narrow palate suggest difficult laryngoscopy, as does a stiff mandibular space. A TMD above 6 cm is reassuring.

questions.stem: A colleague says, "With a videolaryngoscope, airway exams don't matter anymore." What is the BEST response?
options: VL replaces assessment in elective cases
VL makes the Mallampati score irrelevant but not TMD
questions.explanation: VL has changed the predictive value of traditional tests, but assessment still guides planning and backups.

questions.stem: A student measures from the mandible-neck junction to the thyroid notch. Which measurement is this?
questions.explanation: The modified hyomental distance runs from the mandible-neck junction to the thyroid notch.

questions.stem: A patient has a reassuring Mallampati but a short TMD and limited neck extension. Why use multiple assessments?
options: Each test measures the same structure
questions.explanation: Combining assessments improves accuracy and reduces variability.

questions.stem: Which predict difficult bag-mask ventilation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Predictors include facial hair, edentulous, obesity, elderly, snoring/OSA, Mallampati III/IV.

questions.stem: Which patient has an age-related risk factor for difficult bag-mask ventilation?
options: A 25-year-old with a full set of teeth
A 62-year-old with loss of tissue elasticity
questions.explanation: Age over 55 is associated with difficult mask ventilation because of reduced tissue elasticity.

questions.stem: A patient's BMI is 34. How does this affect your mask ventilation plan?
options: It predicts difficult BMV, since BMI exceeds 30
It does not matter until BMI exceeds 45
It matters when BMI is below 18
questions.explanation: Obesity (BMI over 30) is a predictor of difficult mask ventilation.

questions.stem: During BMV, the chest barely moves, ETCO2 is faint, and SpO2 drifts from 99% to 91%. What do these findings show?
options: Adequate BMV, since SpO2 is above 85%
Adequate BMV, since some ETCO2 is present
questions.explanation: Signs of inadequate BMV include poor chest movement, low or absent ETCO2, poor breath sounds, and SpO2 below 92%.

questions.stem: You are using a structured approach to predict difficult laryngoscopy. Which elements belong in it?
options: Snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, and BMI
Machine, suction, monitors, airway, IV, and drugs
Look externally, 3-3-2, Mallampati, obstruction, and neck mobility
Surgery, hematoma, obesity, radiation, and tumor
questions.explanation: The LEMON-type approach covers external look, 3-3-2, Mallampati, obstruction or obesity, and neck mobility. SHORT predicts difficult cric.

questions.stem: Which predict difficult SGA placement? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: SGA difficulty comes from limited opening, obstruction, distortion, and stiff lungs.

questions.stem: A patient had neck radiation for laryngeal cancer and a prior tracheostomy scar. Which mnemonic captures factors that make cricothyrotomy difficult?
options: SHORT: surgery, hematoma, obesity, radiation, tumor
LEMON: look, evaluate, Mallampati, obstruction, neck
STOP-BANG: snoring, tiredness, apnea, pressure, BMI
MOANS: mask seal, obesity, age, no teeth, stiffness
questions.explanation: SHORT predicts difficult cricothyrotomy: Surgery, Hematoma, Obesity, Radiation, Tumor.

questions.stem: A patient with a large neck mass and prior radiation is scheduled for GA. What should you do before induction?
options: Avoid identifying it to prevent anxiety
Rely on the surgeon to locate it if needed
questions.explanation: In high-risk patients, marking the cricothyroid membrane before induction speeds emergency access.

questions.stem: During a CICO event, a patient has a large neck mass and prior radiation. Is cricothyrotomy contraindicated?
options: Yes; prior radiation is an absolute contraindication
Yes; obesity is an absolute contraindication
Yes; neck masses are an absolute contraindication
questions.explanation: There are no absolute contraindications to emergency cricothyrotomy when the patient cannot be oxygenated.

questions.stem: A trauma patient with neck pain needs a cervical spine evaluation before airway planning. Which imaging is the gold standard for fractures?
questions.explanation: CT is the gold standard for cervical spine fractures.

questions.stem: In a patient with a BMI of 55, you cannot palpate the cricothyroid membrane. What can help?
questions.explanation: POCUS can identify the cricothyroid membrane in obese patients.

questions.stem: An airway ultrasound shows thick pretracheal soft tissue. What does this predict?
questions.explanation: Increased pretracheal soft tissue thickness predicts difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: Your department performs about 44,000 general anesthetics a year. Based on NAP4, about how many major airway complications would you expect?
questions.explanation: NAP4 found about 1 major airway complication per 22,000 anesthetics: 44,000 ÷ 22,000 = 2.

questions.stem: Based on NAP4, how many airway-related deaths would you expect in 180,000 anesthetics?
questions.explanation: NAP4 reported about 1 airway death per 180,000 anesthetics.

questions.stem: An obstetric unit performs 600 general anesthetics a year. Based on the estimated CICV rate, about how many CICV events would you expect?
questions.explanation: The obstetric CICV incidence is about 1 in 300: 600 ÷ 300 = 2.

questions.stem: How does the CICV incidence in obstetric patients compare with non-obstetric patients?
questions.explanation: 2,250 ÷ 300 = 7.5, so obstetric CICV is about 7.5 times more common.

questions.stem: In a department doing 2,000 inductions a year, about how many patients will be difficult to mask ventilate?
questions.explanation: Difficult facemask ventilation occurs in about 0.9–7.8% of patients.

questions.stem: In that same department, about how many supraglottic airway insertions will fail?
questions.explanation: SAD failure occurs in about 0.19–1.1% of cases.

questions.stem: Which factors cause SAD failure? (Select 2)
options: Normal dentition with a good seal
questions.explanation: SAD failure is linked to poor seal and table rotation, as well as dentition problems, male sex, and high BMI.

questions.stem: How much more likely are adverse airway events causing death or brain damage in ED or ICU vs OR?
questions.explanation: Adverse airway events are 30–60x more likely in ED/ICU.

questions.stem: A paramedic program reviews prehospital airway data. Up to what percentage of prehospital airway cases require emergency cricothyrotomy?
questions.explanation: Emergency cricothyrotomy rates in prehospital settings can reach 11%.

questions.stem: A patient with a supraglottic tumor is scheduled for laryngoscopy and biopsy. Roughly how often is intubation difficult in pharyngolaryngeal disease?
questions.explanation: Difficult intubation occurred in about 28% of patients with pharyngolaryngeal disease.

questions.stem: A patient with a normal preop airway exam cannot be intubated, and the scope shows a large mass at the base of the tongue. What is the MOST likely hidden cause?
questions.explanation: Lingual tonsil hyperplasia can cause unanticipated difficult or failed airways despite a normal exam.

questions.stem: Which clues suggest lingual tonsil hyperplasia? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Lingual tonsil hyperplasia presents with sore throat and globus sensation, along with dysphagia, snoring, and OSA.

questions.stem: You are inducing a healthy adult for an elective case with an ETT. Which sequence is standard?
options: NMB, propofol, DL, BMV, then preoxygenate
Preoxygenate, NMB, propofol, BMV, then DL
Preoxygenate, propofol, BMV, NMB, then DL
Propofol, NMB, preoxygenate, DL, then BMV
questions.explanation: The standard sequence is preoxygenation, induction agent, confirming mask ventilation, NMB, then laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, nitrogen in the FRC is replaced by oxygen. What is preoxygenation also called?
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation is also described as nitrogen washout or denitrogenation.

questions.stem: How long of a safe apneic time can preoxygenation provide in healthy patients with normal FRC?
questions.explanation: Up to 8 minutes of safe apnea in healthy patients.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, expired O2 rises to 75%. Per this lecture, has the goal been met? (Phases of GA used a higher target.)
questions.explanation: This lecture lists an expired O2 goal above 70%; the Phases lecture used about 90%.

questions.stem: A cooperative patient is being preoxygenated before an elective induction. Which technique is correct?
options: Loose mask with room air for 5 minutes
Nasal cannula at 2 L/min for 1 minute before induction
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation needs a good seal, high-flow 100% O2, and large tidal breaths for 3–5 minutes.

questions.stem: A patient needs urgent induction and there is no time for 3 minutes of tidal breathing. Which alternative preoxygenation technique works?
questions.explanation: Eight vital capacity breaths in 60 seconds is an accepted alternative to 3–5 minutes of tidal breathing.

questions.stem: After induction, intubation fails twice and SpO2 is falling. Which skill becomes your initial rescue?
options: Repeated DL with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: BMV is arguably the most important airway skill and the initial rescue maneuver.

questions.stem: A student pushes the mask hard onto the face and gets a poor seal with no chest rise. What is the correct technique?
options: Pressing the mask firmly down onto the face
Holding the mask loosely to avoid pressure
Using the chin as a fulcrum for the thumb
C-E grip, pulling the jaw up into the mask
questions.explanation: The C-E grip lifts the mandible into the mask; pressing down pushes the jaw back and worsens obstruction.

questions.stem: Which signs confirm effective BMV? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Look for chest rise, fog, and ETCO2.

questions.stem: What should be considered for patients with thick necks, beards, or OSA during BMV?
options: A smaller mask with higher oxygen flow
Oral airway and two-hand mask technique
Higher pressure with a one-hand grip
Smaller mask with a tight seal
questions.explanation: Consider an OA and two-hand mask.

questions.stem: After induction, BMV is inadequate with no chest rise. What is the FIRST step?
questions.explanation: Repositioning is the first step in BMV escalation, before adjuncts or devices.

questions.stem: After induction, BMV is inadequate. Which escalation sequence is correct?
options: OPA, cric, reposition, SGA, then ETT as the final step
SGA, reposition, OPA, cric, then ETT
Cric, SGA, OPA, reposition, then ETT
Reposition, OPA, two-hand seal, SGA or ETT, then cric
questions.explanation: Escalate from repositioning to an OPA, a two-hand seal, then an SGA or ETT, and cric if all fail.

questions.stem: One provider cannot seal the mask on a bearded, obese patient. Refer to the two-person BMV figure. What is the advantage?
options: It replaces the need for adjuncts
questions.explanation: Two-person BMV lets one provider use both hands for the seal and jaw thrust while the other bags.

questions.stem: An obese, edentulous patient with an NG tube is predicted to be difficult to mask. Which steps improve BMV? (Select 3)
options: Leaving dentures in if they improve the seal
Considering removal of the NG tube
questions.explanation: Ramping, keeping dentures in when they help the seal, removing an NG tube, and preparing alternatives all improve BMV.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman at term and a BMI 50 patient desaturate within 60 seconds of apnea. What do they share?
questions.explanation: Obesity and pregnancy reduce FRC, shrinking the oxygen reserve.

questions.stem: During apneic oxygenation, oxygen keeps entering the lungs even though the patient is not breathing. What is the mechanism?
options: Residual negative pressure from the last breath
questions.explanation: Oxygen is absorbed faster than CO2 returns, creating a pressure gradient that draws oxygen in.

questions.stem: How much CO2 enters the alveoli per minute during apnea?
questions.explanation: Only ~8–20 mL/min CO2 enters alveoli.

questions.stem: You plan apneic oxygenation during an RSI. What nasal cannula flow is used?
questions.explanation: Standard nasal cannula at 15 L/min is used for apneic oxygenation.

questions.stem: During apneic oxygenation, SpO2 still falls quickly in a patient with severe tongue obstruction. Which requirement is not met?
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation requires a patent upper airway for oxygen to reach the alveoli.

questions.stem: After 8 minutes of apneic oxygenation, SpO2 is 95% but the ABG shows pH 7.15. What explains this?
options: CO2 builds up without ventilation, causing acidosis
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation maintains oxygenation but not ventilation, so CO2 accumulates.

questions.stem: A standard nasal cannula is used at 15 L/min for a prolonged period. Which complication becomes more likely?
questions.explanation: High-flow oxygen should be short-term to avoid airway mucosal damage.

questions.stem: Which patients benefit MOST from apneic oxygenation?
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation is most useful in obese patients or during prolonged attempts.

questions.stem: After induction, BMV is difficult with snoring sounds despite a jaw thrust. What is the BEST next step?
options: Insert an OPA to relieve tongue obstruction
Insert an NPA to confirm tracheal placement
Wait to insert an OPA until after intubation
Insert an NPA to prevent laryngospasm
questions.explanation: An oral airway relieves tongue obstruction when BMV is inadequate.

questions.stem: A colleague says, "I did a VL." What distinguishes DL and VL from TI?
options: DL places the tube; VL visualizes
questions.explanation: DL and VL describe how the larynx is visualized; TI is passing the tube through the cords.

questions.stem: You use a Miller blade on a child with a floppy epiglottis. Where should the tip be placed?
options: At the base of the tongue
questions.explanation: The straight Miller blade lifts the epiglottis directly.

questions.stem: With a Macintosh blade in the vallecula, how is the epiglottis lifted?
questions.explanation: The Mac blade lifts the epiglottis indirectly via the hyoepiglottic ligament.

questions.stem: What should be avoided during laryngoscopy?
options: Levering the blade against the teeth
Sweeping the tongue to the left side
questions.explanation: Levering on teeth risks damage.

questions.stem: During DL, the view improves when an assistant presses the thyroid cartilage back, up, and to the right. What is this maneuver?
questions.explanation: BURP is backward, upward, and rightward pressure on the thyroid cartilage to improve the view.

questions.stem: During BURP, the assistant pushes the thyroid cartilage backward, rightward, and "upward." Which direction is upward?
questions.explanation: In BURP, upward means cephalad, toward the head.

questions.stem: The ETT tip is pressed against the tracheal wall, but ventilation continues. Which feature allows this?
questions.explanation: The Murphy eye provides a distal opening if the tip is obstructed.

questions.stem: A cuff manometer reads 40 cmH2O 2 hours into a case. What should you do?
options: Leave it, since higher pressure prevents aspiration
questions.explanation: Cuff pressure should not exceed 25 cmH2O to avoid tracheal mucosal injury.

questions.stem: During a nitrous oxide anesthetic, the cuff pressure rises from 22 to 38 cmH2O over an hour. What explains this?
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide diffuses into air-filled cuffs and raises their pressure.

questions.stem: You are selecting oral ETT sizes for an average-sized woman and man. Which pairing is typical?
questions.explanation: Typical adult sizes are 6.5–7.0 mm for women and 7.0–7.5 mm for men.

questions.stem: A patient is intubated with a 6.0 ETT instead of a 7.0. By Poiseuille's law, about how much does airway resistance increase?
questions.explanation: Resistance varies with 1/r⁴: (7/6)⁴ ≈ 1.85, about 85% higher.

questions.stem: A patient needs a vocal cord polyp excision, and the surgeon needs maximal view of the cords. Which ETT is designed for this?
questions.explanation: Microlaryngeal tubes are small-diameter, full-length tubes for laryngeal surgery.

questions.stem: A patient will be prone with the head turned for a spine case. Which ETT resists kinking?
questions.explanation: Armored tubes contain a wire coil that resists kinking.

questions.stem: A patient needs a lobectomy requiring one-lung ventilation. Which tube allows this?
questions.explanation: Double-lumen tubes isolate and ventilate each lung separately.

questions.stem: You want continuous visualization of the tube position during a thoracic case without a bronchoscope. Which tube has an integrated camera?
options: A double-lumen tube with a bronchial cuff
questions.explanation: The VivaSight ETT has an integrated camera.

questions.stem: For which patients are uncuffed ETTs traditionally used?
questions.explanation: Uncuffed ETTs have traditionally been used in neonates and infants.

questions.stem: You place a folded towel under the head and extend at the atlantooccipital joint. What position is this?
questions.explanation: The sniffing position combines neck flexion with atlantooccipital extension.

questions.stem: What aids alignment in difficult cases?
questions.explanation: Use pillows, towels, or ramping.

questions.stem: During DL with a Macintosh blade, where is the blade inserted initially?
options: Into the right side of the mouth
Into the left side of the mouth
questions.explanation: The curved blade enters on the right and sweeps the tongue to the left.

questions.stem: During laryngoscopy, the student rocks the blade back on the upper teeth. How should the blade be lifted instead?
questions.explanation: Lift along the handle at about 45° forward without levering on the teeth.

questions.stem: You plan nasal intubation. How should you select the nostril?
options: Use the right nostril by default
Use the left nostril by default
questions.explanation: Testing airflow through each nostril helps choose the more patent side.

questions.stem: Before nasal intubation, which drugs reduce bleeding?
questions.explanation: Topical vasoconstrictors such as phenylephrine or oxymetazoline reduce nasal bleeding.

questions.stem: How should the bevel be oriented during nasal insertion?
questions.explanation: Bevel away from midline reduces turbinate avulsion risk.

questions.stem: During nasal intubation, the tube meets resistance high in the nose. Along which path should it advance?
options: Along the floor of the nose
Toward the top of the nose
questions.explanation: The nasal ETT should advance along the floor of the nose below the inferior turbinate.

questions.stem: During nasal intubation, at about what depth does the ETT reach the oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The nasal ETT typically reaches the oropharynx at about 14–16 cm.

questions.stem: You use Magill forceps to guide a nasal ETT into the larynx. Where should you grasp the tube?
questions.explanation: Grasp the tube proximal to the cuff to avoid tearing it.

questions.stem: A patient with limited mouth opening needs nasal intubation for a dental case. Which techniques can be used? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Nasal intubation can be blind, VL-assisted, or fiberoptic.

questions.stem: A patient has a fractured mandible with wired teeth. When is nasotracheal intubation useful?
options: When oral intubation is difficult or impossible
When the patient has a basilar skull fracture
questions.explanation: Nasotracheal intubation is useful when oral access is limited, such as mandibular fractures.

questions.stem: A patient will be intubated for a 6-hour case. Which cuff design on a standard adult ETT reduces tracheal mucosal injury?
questions.explanation: Standard ETTs use high-volume, low-pressure cuffs that spread pressure over more tracheal surface.

questions.stem: The ETT's proximal end connects to the breathing circuit. Which part allows this?
questions.explanation: The 15-mm adapter connects the ETT to the circuit.

questions.stem: On chest X-ray, an ETT tip sits 1 cm above the carina. Where should it ideally be?
questions.explanation: The ETT tip should sit mid-trachea, above the carina, to avoid endobronchial migration.

questions.stem: During induction, mask ventilation is hard, the laryngoscopic view is poor, and a front-of-neck approach looks difficult. Which term describes any of these problems?
options: Failed airway after one attempt at DL
A Mallampati IV airway found on the preoperative exam
questions.explanation: A difficult airway involves trouble with mask ventilation, SGA, laryngoscopy, intubation, extubation, or invasive access.

questions.stem: After three intubation attempts and inadequate mask ventilation, SpO2 is 80%. What term applies?
options: A difficult airway that needs a bougie on the first pass
Failed airway: unable to intubate or ventilate after multiple attempts
questions.explanation: A failed airway is the inability to intubate or ventilate after multiple attempts and requires immediate rescue.

questions.stem: Which are the four key airway management strategies? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The four are mask ventilation, SGA, tracheal intubation, and invasive airway.

questions.stem: Four patients present for emergency surgery. Which features cause a difficult airway? (Select 3)
options: An expanding neck hematoma after thyroidectomy
Severe hypoxia or hypotension limiting safe apnea time
questions.explanation: Difficult airway causes are anatomic, pathophysiologic, traumatic, and physiologic, including shock and hypoxia that shorten safe apnea time.

questions.stem: Which signs suggest difficult ventilation? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Difficult ventilation shows as mask leak and gastric insufflation, along with poor chest rise, SpO2 under 92%, and the need for two hands or adjuncts.

questions.stem: An LMA has a leak at 12 cmH2O. What does this suggest?
options: A normal seal for most patients
questions.explanation: A leak pressure under 15 cmH2O suggests difficult supraglottic airway ventilation.

questions.stem: Using the Airway Approach Algorithm for a patient with a minor procedure, what question is asked FIRST?
options: Can the patient be intubated awake?
questions.explanation: The first question is whether airway management is needed at all.

questions.stem: Which are the Airway Approach Algorithm's five questions? (Select 4)
options: Is the patient at risk of aspiration?
Is DL/VL and intubation expected to be difficult?
Is the patient at risk of rapid desaturation?
questions.explanation: Five questions: necessity, difficulty, supralaryngeal ventilation, aspiration risk, rapid desaturation.

questions.stem: A pre-induction airway algorithm identifies several major concerns. Which response best follows the algorithm rather than forcing a routine induction?
questions.explanation: Concern on any question prompts alternative plans.

questions.stem: When should planning for a predicted difficult airway begin?
questions.explanation: Airway planning should begin before induction of anesthesia.

questions.stem: A department wants to adopt a difficult airway algorithm. Which algorithms are commonly referenced?
questions.explanation: The ASA algorithm and DAS guidelines are the major difficult airway algorithms.

questions.stem: Why are difficult airway algorithms based mostly on expert consensus rather than RCTs?
options: Outcomes vary too much between countries
Events are too rare for RCTs
questions.explanation: Critical airway events are rare, so randomized trials are difficult, and algorithms rely on consensus.

questions.stem: You are planning an awake intubation for a patient with a known difficult airway and severe OSA. How should opioids be used for sedation?
options: Avoid or minimize them to protect spontaneous ventilation
Use them because they preserve ventilatory drive
Use them as the required core of awake sedation
questions.explanation: With a difficult airway, avoid opioids that can cause apnea and loss of the airway before it is secured.

questions.stem: A patient with a large mediastinal mass and stridor needs intubation. What is the main principle guiding your technique?
options: Use deep neuromuscular blockade for a still field
Use controlled ventilation with deep paralysis
Prioritize opioid analgesia for comfort during laryngoscopy
Preserve spontaneous ventilation, such as with awake intubation
questions.explanation: In difficult airways, preserving spontaneous ventilation keeps a safety margin if the airway cannot be secured.

questions.stem: Why does meticulous preoxygenation matter more when a difficult airway is predicted?
options: It increases tidal volume after induction
It increases the oxygen reservoir in FRC and extends safe apnea time
It stores CO2 to restore respiratory drive
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation replaces nitrogen in the FRC with oxygen, and apneic oxygenation prolongs time to desaturation.

questions.stem: Which components belong on a difficult airway cart? (Select 4)
options: Several laryngoscope blade types and sizes
questions.explanation: Core components include laryngoscopy tools, alternative devices, confirmation tools, and airway anesthesia.

questions.stem: A difficult airway cart is being stocked. Which items are optional additions rather than core contents?
questions.explanation: VL and flexible scopes are optional additions to the core difficult airway cart.

questions.stem: A patient is expected to be difficult to intubate, and losing spontaneous ventilation could make rescue impossible. Which airway strategy best preserves safety?
options: Routine IV induction and direct laryngoscopy
Rapid-sequence induction because the stomach may be full
Deep sedation without securing the airway
Awake intubation while maintaining spontaneous ventilation
questions.explanation: Awake intubation is used when difficult airway is anticipated and spontaneous ventilation must be maintained.

questions.stem: Which conditions support awake intubation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Indications include prior difficulty, unstable C-spine, tumors, trauma, burns, OSA, and limited opening.

questions.stem: Which are advantages of awake intubation? (Select 2)
options: Removes the need for topical anesthesia
questions.explanation: Awake intubation preserves spontaneous breathing and muscle tone, as well as airway reflexes. It takes more time and preparation.

questions.stem: Which antisialagogues are used for awake intubation?
questions.explanation: Antisialagogues dry secretions.

questions.stem: You are topicalizing the airway of a 70 kg patient for awake intubation with lidocaine nebulizer, spray, and blocks. What maximum total dose should you stay under?
questions.explanation: Estimate a maximum of about 4–5 mg/kg IV equivalent, or 280–350 mg for 70 kg, counting every route.

questions.stem: Which sedation caution is emphasized for awake intubation?
options: Avoid deep sedation that may collapse the airway
Use deep sedation to prevent coughing
questions.explanation: Deep sedation may cause airway collapse.

questions.stem: Which sedatives are optional for awake intubation?
questions.explanation: Optional sedation includes dexmedetomidine, midazolam, or fentanyl.

questions.stem: A patient with GERD and a full stomach needs an awake intubation. Which aspiration prophylaxis agents are appropriate? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: A nonparticulate antacid, a gastrokinetic, and an H2 antagonist reduce aspiration risk and harm.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve supplies the posterior 1/3 of the tongue and oropharynx?
questions.explanation: CN IX supplies posterior tongue, oropharynx, and upper larynx.

questions.stem: After intubation, loss of sensation below the vocal cords would most directly implicate which nerve?
questions.explanation: The RLN supplies below the cords and trachea.

questions.stem: Topical anesthesia of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue must cover sensation carried primarily by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve (V3) supplies the anterior tongue.

questions.stem: For awake nasal intubation, which nerve branches are most directly targeted to anesthetize the nasal passages?
options: Anterior ethmoidal, nasopalatine, and sphenopalatine nerves
questions.explanation: Nasal anesthesia targets trigeminal branches.

questions.stem: What dose is used in a nebulizer for airway topicalization?
options: 20 mL of 2% lidocaine with no vasoconstrictor added
4–10 mL of 4% lidocaine plus 1 mL of 1% phenylephrine
questions.explanation: Nebulizer: 4–10 mL 4% lidocaine + 1 mL 1% phenylephrine.

questions.stem: How long does nebulized topicalization take?
questions.explanation: Nebulization requires 10–20 minutes.

questions.stem: What risk is associated with benzocaine topical spray?
questions.explanation: Benzocaine carries a risk of methemoglobinemia.

questions.stem: During awake airway topicalization, 5% lidocaine paste is applied to a tongue blade against the posterior tongue. Which technique is being used?
options: Lidocaine jelly on the ETT cuff
questions.explanation: It anesthetizes the posterior tongue, vallecula, and epiglottis.

questions.stem: Where is the needle placed for a glossopharyngeal block?
options: Greater cornu of the hyoid bone
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal block is at the base of the palatoglossal arch.

questions.stem: During a glossopharyngeal block, blood is aspirated. What should you do?
options: Stop and switch to general anesthesia immediately
Reposition medially to avoid the carotid artery
Inject anyway at a slower rate
questions.explanation: Blood means reposition medially to avoid the carotid.

questions.stem: During a glossopharyngeal block, air is aspirated. What does it mean?
options: The needle is in the esophagus
The needle is too deep; withdraw
The needle is in the carotid
The needle is in the correct place
questions.explanation: Air means too deep.

questions.stem: How much lidocaine is injected per side for a glossopharyngeal block?
questions.explanation: Inject 1–2 mL of 2% lidocaine per side.

questions.stem: What landmark is used for the superior laryngeal nerve block?
options: Greater cornu of the hyoid bone
questions.explanation: The SLN block uses the greater cornu of the hyoid.

questions.stem: A superior laryngeal nerve block is intended to anesthetize supraglottic sensation. Which branch must be blocked?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The internal branch provides supraglottic sensation.

questions.stem: What region does the SLN block anesthetize?
options: Anterior tongue and floor of the mouth
questions.explanation: The SLN block anesthetizes the supraglottic region.

questions.stem: For a superior laryngeal nerve block, which injection sequence best matches the technique described in the lecture?
options: Inject 1 mL above the membrane, advance 2–3 mm, then inject 2 mL
Inject 5 mL through the cricothyroid membrane
Inject 1 mL into the palatoglossal arch
questions.explanation: Inject 1 mL above the membrane, then advance and inject 2 mL more.

questions.stem: Where is the transtracheal block performed?
options: At the base of the tongue
At the greater cornu of the hyoid
questions.explanation: The transtracheal block goes through the cricothyroid membrane.

questions.stem: What confirms needle placement in the transtracheal block?
options: A loss of resistance to saline
questions.explanation: Air aspiration confirms tracheal placement.

questions.stem: When is local anesthetic injected during a transtracheal block?
options: During expiration, to avoid a cough
questions.explanation: Inject during inspiration; the cough spreads anesthetic.

questions.stem: How much lidocaine is used for a transtracheal block?
questions.explanation: A syringe with 3–5 mL of 2% lidocaine is used.

questions.stem: Why is an angiocatheter preferred in the transtracheal block?
options: It gives faster onset of anesthesia at the cords
It prevents the patient from coughing
A softer catheter reduces trauma during coughing
questions.explanation: A softer angiocatheter reduces mucosal injury.

questions.stem: What nerves does the transtracheal block anesthetize?
options: Recurrent laryngeal distribution below the cords
questions.explanation: It anesthetizes the trachea and cords (RLN region).

questions.stem: Which block combination provides full awake intubation anesthesia?
options: Transtracheal block alone for the whole airway
Topical plus glossopharyngeal, SLN, and transtracheal blocks
Glossopharyngeal block alone for the whole airway
SLN block alone for the whole upper airway
questions.explanation: Combining topical and nerve blocks provides complete anesthesia.

questions.stem: During an RSI, an assistant applies pressure to the cricoid cartilage to occlude the esophagus. Who first described this maneuver, and when?
questions.explanation: Sellick described cricoid pressure in 1961. Macintosh designed the curved blade, and Brain the LMA.

questions.stem: What cricoid pressure does this lecture recommend before loss of consciousness?
questions.explanation: 10–20 N before LOC, 30–40 N after.

questions.stem: What cricoid pressure does this lecture recommend after loss of consciousness?
questions.explanation: 30–40 N after LOC.

questions.stem: As originally described, how was the patient positioned when cricoid pressure was applied?
questions.explanation: Sellick described cricoid pressure with the patient in a 20-degree head-up position.

questions.stem: Why does MRI evidence weaken the assumption that cricoid pressure reliably compresses the esophagus?
options: The esophagus is displaced laterally in many patients
The esophagus is completely occluded in nearly all patients
The esophagus does not change position
The trachea collapses in most patients
questions.explanation: MRI shows the esophagus shifts laterally in 50–90%.

questions.stem: What risk arises from cricoid pressure above 40 N?
options: Hypertension and tachycardia from sympathetic surge
questions.explanation: Excessive pressure can cause discomfort or retching.

questions.stem: During an RSI, the assistant's cricoid pressure is pushing the larynx down and to the side. Which complications can result? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Cricoid pressure can obstruct the airway, impair ventilation and the view, and prolong intubation.

questions.stem: What is compared to firm pressure on the bridge of the nose?
questions.explanation: Recommended cricoid pressure feels like firm pressure on the nasal bridge.

questions.stem: What are the indications for supraglottic devices? (Select 3)
options: Alternative to ETT for elective surgery
Protection against aspiration in full stomach
questions.explanation: SGDs are for rescue, elective use, and as an intubation conduit.

questions.stem: When was the LMA introduced?
questions.explanation: The LMA was introduced in 1981 and used widely in the US since 1989.

questions.stem: An experienced CRNA places an LMA for a knee arthroscopy. How often does the first attempt typically succeed?
questions.explanation: First-attempt LMA success for experienced providers is about 88–95%.

questions.stem: What LMA cuff pressure should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Avoid overinflation >60 cmH2O, which can open the esophagus.

questions.stem: Standard LMA insertion fails twice because the tip folds. Which alternative techniques can help? (Select 4)
options: Insertion with the cuff fully inflated
questions.explanation: Alternatives include tongue blade help, 180-degree rotation, partial inflation, and guided insertion.

questions.stem: What improvements do second-generation SGAs have? (Select 4)
options: Enhanced cuff design for higher seal pressures
questions.explanation: Second-gen SGAs add gastric channels, reinforced tips, better cuffs, and more rigidity.

questions.stem: What seal pressure does the LMA ProSeal support?
questions.explanation: ProSeal supports peak pressures up to 28–30 cmH2O.

questions.stem: What seal pressure does the LMA Supreme provide?
questions.explanation: The Supreme has slightly lower seal pressures (26–28 cmH2O) than ProSeal.

questions.stem: When counseling about supraglottic airway aspiration risk, which incidence best reflects the low but nonzero event rate?
questions.explanation: Aspiration risk is low, ~1–2 per 10,000.

questions.stem: In which situations should a supraglottic airway be avoided as the primary device? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: SGAs are avoided with subglottic obstruction, active aspiration, and in obstetric patients because they do not protect the airway.

questions.stem: What problems can SGA malposition or cuff overinflation cause? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Malposition or overinflation compromise seal, gastric drainage, and airway patency.

questions.stem: What are the dimensions of the Eschmann bougie?
options: 40 cm long with a 60° angled tip
60 cm long with a 40° angled tip
30 cm long with a 90° angled tip
100 cm long with a straight tip
questions.explanation: The bougie is 60 cm with a 40° tip.

questions.stem: When is a bougie MOST useful?
options: When the glottis is hard to see, like CL IIb or III
When the view is CL grade I with full cords
When the patient is awake and cooperative
For nasal intubation, as a guide through the nose
questions.explanation: Bougies help with poor glottic views.

questions.stem: What confirms bougie placement in the trachea?
questions.explanation: Clicks against tracheal rings suggest tracheal placement.

questions.stem: What depth mark at the lips is ideal for bougie insertion?
questions.explanation: The 25-cm mark at the lips is ideal.

questions.stem: If the ETT meets resistance while railroading over a bougie, what should you do?
options: Remove the bougie and try blind
Rotate the ETT 90° to the left
Rotate the ETT 180° to the right
questions.explanation: Rotate 90° counterclockwise to free the bevel.

questions.stem: What was the Trachlite lighted stylet?
options: A device using neck transillumination for ETT placement
A videolaryngoscope with a lighted blade tip
A fiberoptic scope used for nasal intubation
A bougie with a light at the tip for blind placement
questions.explanation: It used a glow on the anterior neck to confirm tracheal placement.

questions.stem: Why was the Trachlite discontinued?
options: It caused tracheal perforation in most patients
Shift toward fiberoptic and video tools
questions.explanation: It was discontinued in 2009 as fiberoptic and video tools took over.

questions.stem: Where should an airway exchange catheter tip sit?
questions.explanation: AEC tips are placed just above the carina.

questions.stem: What sizes of AEC are well tolerated in adults?
questions.explanation: 11F and 14F are well tolerated.

questions.stem: Why can an airway exchange catheter be safer to leave temporarily after difficult extubation than a bougie?
options: It can permit breathing, phonation, and secretion clearance
It is intentionally much stiffer than a bougie
It must be removed immediately after extubation
It cannot serve as a guide for reintubation
questions.explanation: AECs allow spontaneous breathing, speech, and secretion clearance.

questions.stem: Why might muscle relaxation be needed with jet ventilation through an AEC?
questions.explanation: Muscle relaxation can prevent glottic closure during jet insufflation.

questions.stem: What should be matched when reintubating over an AEC?
options: ETT cuff pressure to the AEC size
ETT curvature to the AEC curvature at the glottis
ETT internal diameter to AEC external diameter
ETT length to AEC length for depth
questions.explanation: Match ETT ID to AEC OD.

questions.stem: Which are indications for flexible scope intubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: FIS is indicated for anticipated difficult airways, C-spine immobilization, restricted opening, and failed intubation with ventilation.

questions.stem: When should FIS be avoided? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Avoid in epiglottitis, burns, trauma, uncooperative or hypoxic patients, and CICV.

questions.stem: How is lateral movement of the FIS controlled?
questions.explanation: The lever controls up/down; wrist rotation controls lateral movement.

questions.stem: Oxygen is insufflated through the suction port during flexible-scope intubation. Which benefit is most useful during a prolonged attempt?
options: Support oxygenation and clear the lens
questions.explanation: O2 insufflation at 2–4 L/min helps oxygenation and clears the lens.

questions.stem: Which oral airways protect the FIS from biting?
questions.explanation: FIS-compatible oral airways include Williams and Ovassapian.

questions.stem: How can FIS fogging be reduced?
options: Warm saline soak or antifog agent
questions.explanation: Warm saline or antifog agents help.

questions.stem: Which are advantages of videolaryngoscopy? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: VL offers magnified view, team viewing, and easier learning.

questions.stem: Which are disadvantages of videolaryngoscopy? (Select 2)
options: View obscured by blood or secretions
Inability to use a stylet with the tube
questions.explanation: VL is costly, and blood or secretions can obscure the camera. Blind tube advancement past the tonsils can injure the pharynx.

questions.stem: What pharyngeal injury is specifically noted with VL?
options: Soft palate or tonsillar pillar perforation
Vocal cord paralysis from nerve stretch
questions.explanation: Indirect ETT/stylet placement can perforate the soft palate or pillars.

questions.stem: A new graduate plans to use only videolaryngoscopy for every intubation. What is the BEST advice?
options: Keep skills in both DL and VL, since either can be the rescue
VL has fully replaced DL in modern practice
Use DL as the primary device and VL only for rescue
VL should be reserved for airway experts
questions.explanation: Proficiency in both DL and VL is needed, since either may be the rescue technique when the other fails.

questions.stem: Why is a standard straight stylet poorly matched to a hyperangulated GlideScope blade?
options: The blade has only a slight 15° curve
The tube must approximate the blade's steep anterior curvature
questions.explanation: The hyperangulated blade has a 60° anterior bend.

questions.stem: How does GlideScope prevent fogging?
questions.explanation: GlideScope uses a heated lens.

questions.stem: How does the McGrath prevent fogging?
options: Heated lens that warms the camera
questions.explanation: McGrath uses a hydrophilic coating rather than a heater.

questions.stem: Which VL device offers standard Mac/Miller geometry plus hyperangulated blades with video recording?
questions.explanation: The C-MAC offers standard and hyperangulated blades and recording.

questions.stem: Which VL device is highly portable with a built-in monitor?
questions.explanation: McGrath has a self-contained rotatable LCD.

questions.stem: When using a hyperangulated GlideScope, what tube preparation is recommended?
options: No stylet and a straight, unshaped tube
questions.explanation: Use a rigid stylet or preshaped ETT.

questions.stem: You insert a GlideScope and keep looking in the mouth, but the tip passes the epiglottis and the view is lost. What technique would have helped?
options: Insert to the right and sweep the tongue
Insert midline and look at the monitor early
Insert laterally and look in the mouth first
questions.explanation: Insert the GlideScope midline and shift to the monitor early to avoid passing structures.

questions.stem: What situation is front-of-neck access designed for?
options: Routine difficult intubation with good ventilation
Nasal intubation failure with good mask ventilation
questions.explanation: FONA is a rescue for CICO.

questions.stem: Which are indications for cricothyrotomy? (Select 3)
options: Facial or neck trauma preventing oral/nasal access
questions.explanation: Indications include CICO, trauma preventing access, and immediate obstruction.

questions.stem: Which are the three cricothyrotomy techniques? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Techniques are needle, percutaneous, and surgical.

questions.stem: What catheter size is recommended for needle cricothyrotomy?
options: 24G IV catheter from the standard IV cart
questions.explanation: Use a large-bore (≥18G) kink-resistant catheter.

questions.stem: Why avoid standard IV angiocaths for TTJV?
options: They are too short to reach the trachea
They are too large for the cricothyroid membrane
questions.explanation: Standard angiocaths risk kinking.

questions.stem: What oxygen source pressure is used for TTJV?
questions.explanation: Jet injectors use high-pressure O2 at 50–100 psi.

questions.stem: What rate is used for TTJV breaths?
questions.explanation: Deliver low-frequency breaths at 8–10/min.

questions.stem: What I:E ratio is recommended for TTJV?
questions.explanation: I:E ratio is 1:3 to 1:4.

questions.stem: What inspiratory time is recommended for TTJV?
questions.explanation: Inspiratory time is 0.5–1 sec.

questions.stem: Why must you ensure chest recoil before the next TTJV breath?
options: To increase oxygen delivery on the next breath
To prevent air trapping and barotrauma
questions.explanation: Exhalation is passive via the upper airway; incomplete exhalation causes air trapping.

questions.stem: During transtracheal jet ventilation, which complication is most immediately life-threatening if exhalation is inadequate?
questions.explanation: Barotrauma is the most serious concern.

questions.stem: During transtracheal jet ventilation through a cricothyroid catheter in a patient with upper airway obstruction, which complications can occur? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: TTJV risks barotrauma, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, and hypercarbia.

questions.stem: How is exhalation achieved during TTJV?
questions.explanation: Exhalation is passive via the upper airway.

questions.stem: What equipment is used for retrograde intubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Equipment includes a catheter, wire/suture, Magill forceps, and ETT.

questions.stem: In retrograde intubation, which direction is the needle angled?
questions.explanation: The needle is angled cephalad.

questions.stem: When is retrograde intubation useful?
options: Visual intubation fails but ventilation is adequate
CICO with no ventilation possible at all
Routine elective intubation in a healthy patient
questions.explanation: It is useful when visual methods fail but ventilation is possible.

questions.stem: At which tracheal rings is a tracheotomy typically performed?
questions.explanation: Tracheotomy is typically at rings 4–6.

questions.stem: Why is tracheotomy not preferred for emergent access?
options: It is less invasive than a cricothyrotomy
It is performed in pediatric patients
It takes up to 30 minutes and needs a surgical team
questions.explanation: Tracheotomy takes time and requires a controlled environment.

questions.stem: Which are tracheotomy complications? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Tracheotomy complications include RLN injury and innominate artery injury, along with esophageal trauma, infection, bleeding, and tracheal stenosis.

questions.stem: What is the target site for all emergency front-of-neck access?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane is the FONA target.

questions.stem: What role does ultrasound play in FONA?
options: Locating the cricothyroid membrane in difficult anatomy
Guiding jet ventilation pressures and the respiratory rate
questions.explanation: Ultrasound helps locate the membrane and may reduce misplacement.

questions.stem: What are the goals of extubation planning? (Select 3)
options: Extubate as early as possible in all cases
questions.explanation: Planning aims to reduce disturbances, complications, stay, and costs.

questions.stem: A patient had an easy intubation for a long neck dissection. A trainee says extubation needs no planning. What is the BEST response?
options: Extubation is lower risk than intubation in most patients
Extubation carries significant risk and needs a plan
Extubation is safer than intubation in every case
questions.explanation: Extubation is not benign. Airway edema, surgery, and residual drugs can make it more dangerous than intubation.

questions.stem: Before extubation, quantitative monitoring shows a TOF ratio of 0.82. Is reversal adequate?
options: Yes; a ratio above 0.3 is adequate here
No; the TOF ratio should exceed 0.9
Yes; a ratio above 0.5 is adequate
Yes; a ratio above 0.7 is adequate
questions.explanation: Adequate reversal requires a TOF ratio greater than 0.9.

questions.stem: Which neuromuscular tests are in the extubation criteria? (Select 5)
options: Head lift for more than 5 seconds
Sustained tetanus at 100 Hz for 5 seconds
questions.explanation: Criteria include TOFR >0.9, 100 Hz tetanus 5 s, DBS without fade, 5-s head lift, and strong grip.

questions.stem: A 70 kg patient's vital capacity before extubation is 900 mL. Does this meet criteria?
options: No; it should exceed 30 mL/kg, or 2,100 mL
No; it should exceed 15 mL/kg, or 1,050 mL
questions.explanation: Vital capacity should exceed 15 mL/kg; 900 mL is about 13 mL/kg.

questions.stem: A patient's negative inspiratory force is −14 cmH2O before planned extubation. How should you interpret it?
options: Inadequate; NIF should be more negative than −60 cmH2O
Adequate; NIF should be more positive than +20 cmH2O
Inadequate; NIF should be more negative than −20 cmH2O
Adequate; it is more negative than −5 cmH2O
questions.explanation: NIF should be more negative than −20 cmH2O before extubation.

questions.stem: An 80 kg patient breathes spontaneously with tidal volumes of 250 mL before extubation. Does this meet criteria?
options: No; tidal volume should be at least 15 mL/kg
No; tidal volume should be at least 4–5 mL/kg (320–400 mL)
No; tidal volume should be at least 10–12 mL/kg
questions.explanation: Spontaneous tidal volume should be at least 4–5 mL/kg; 250 mL is about 3 mL/kg.

questions.stem: On FiO2 0.4, a patient has SpO2 93% and PaO2 72 mmHg before extubation. Do these meet the oxygenation criteria?
options: Yes; criteria are SpO2 above 90% and PaO2 above 60 on FiO2 under 50%
No; SpO2 must exceed 99% and PaO2 200
No; PaO2 must exceed 100 mmHg on any FiO2 before extubation
questions.explanation: Oxygenation criteria for extubation are SpO2 above 90% and PaO2 above 60 mmHg with FiO2 below 50%.
