questions.stem: Which global criteria are required for extubation? (Select 4)
options: Return of laryngeal and cough reflexes
questions.explanation: Global criteria include hemodynamic stability, normothermia, patent airway with reflexes, strength, and metabolic stability.

questions.stem: A patient meets all criteria and is extubated, then struggles to breathe within minutes. What does this show about extubation?
options: It tests neuromuscular function and nothing else
It carries no risk once criteria are met
questions.explanation: Extubation itself tests whether spontaneous ventilation and cardiopulmonary function can be sustained.

questions.stem: During which Guedel stage should extubation be avoided?
questions.explanation: Avoid extubation in stage II due to laryngospasm risk.

questions.stem: When should extubation be performed?
options: Deeply anesthetized (stage III) or fully awake
During stage II excitement, as reflexes return
As soon as spontaneous breathing starts
questions.explanation: Extubate deep in stage III or fully awake.

questions.stem: When should high-risk patients be extubated?
options: Deep in stage III to avoid any coughing on the tube
When reflexes return and ventilation is adequate
questions.explanation: High-risk patients should be extubated awake with reflexes and adequate ventilation.

questions.stem: Which drugs reduce cardiovascular stimulation during awake extubation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, CCBs, and vasodilators blunt the response.

questions.stem: Which drugs minimize coughing and straining at extubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics and cautious opioids reduce coughing.

questions.stem: What proportion of airway emergencies occur during extubation or recovery?
questions.explanation: Up to 1/3 of airway emergencies occur at extubation/recovery.

questions.stem: Which extubation techniques are used for high-risk patients? (Select 4)
options: Use of an airway exchange catheter
questions.explanation: Options include FIS, SGA exchange, AEC, or delayed extubation.

questions.stem: What should be done before extubating a difficult airway?
options: Avoid telling the team to reduce anxiety
Discuss contingency plans with the team
questions.explanation: Always discuss contingency plans with the OR team before extubation.

questions.stem: Which patient risk factors predict difficult extubation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Patient risk factors include difficult reintubation evaluation, illnesses, edema, cervical limitation, and tracheomalacia.

questions.stem: Which surgical risk factors predict difficult extubation? (Select 5)
options: Airway or head and neck surgery
questions.explanation: Surgical risk factors include airway/head and neck surgery, neurosurgery, prolonged duration, and prone/Trendelenburg.

questions.stem: Which anesthetic risk factors predict difficult extubation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Anesthetic factors include difficult intubation, excessive fluids, lack of cuff leak, and laryngotracheal edema.

questions.stem: Why is a lack of cuff leak concerning before extubation?
questions.explanation: Lack of cuff leak suggests laryngotracheal edema.

questions.stem: Which complications result from residual neuromuscular blockade? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Residual block causes obstruction, hypoxemia, aspiration risk, blunted hypoxic response, and weakness.

questions.stem: How does sugammadex reverse rocuronium?
options: Cyclodextrin encapsulation that inactivates the drug
questions.explanation: Sugammadex traps and inactivates rocuronium/vecuronium.

questions.stem: After extubation, the patient makes strong inspiratory efforts but no air moves because the vocal cords have forcefully closed. Which process best explains this?
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is involuntary forceful laryngeal contraction.

questions.stem: In what percentage of laryngospasm cases does desaturation occur?
questions.explanation: Desaturation occurs in up to 60%.

questions.stem: Which afferent-efferent pathway most directly mediates laryngospasm?
options: SLN afferent to RLN motor response
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is triggered by vagal stimulation along the SLN→RLN pathway.

questions.stem: Which type of closure is complete obstruction by extrinsic muscles?
questions.explanation: Ball-valve closure (extrinsic muscles) is complete; glottic shutter (intrinsic) is partial.

questions.stem: Which type of closure is partial obstruction by intrinsic muscles?
questions.explanation: Glottic shutter is intrinsic and partial.

questions.stem: Which are causes of laryngospasm? (Select 3)
options: Blood or secretions on the cords
questions.explanation: Causes include manipulation, noxious stimuli, and light anesthesia.

questions.stem: A patient has persistent laryngospasm despite CPAP. The provider applies a forceful jaw thrust plus pressure at the laryngospasm notch. Which maneuver is this?
questions.explanation: Larson maneuver is jaw thrust plus pressure at the laryngospasm notch.

questions.stem: Laryngospasm persists and oxygen saturation continues to fall despite airway-opening maneuvers and positive pressure. Which drug should be given next?
questions.explanation: Give succinylcholine immediately if desaturation persists.

questions.stem: What complication must be prevented after laryngospasm?
questions.explanation: Address hypoxia and prevent NPPE.

questions.stem: A child develops inspiratory stridor after extubation from subglottic airway swelling. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Croup is subglottic inflammation and edema.

questions.stem: Which signs characterize postextubation croup? (Select 2)
options: Expiratory wheeze with a prolonged I:E ratio
questions.explanation: Postextubation croup causes inspiratory stridor and a barking cough from subglottic edema.

questions.stem: When does postextubation croup typically occur?
questions.explanation: Croup typically occurs within 3 hours.

questions.stem: Which are causes of postextubation croup? (Select 4)
options: Airway edema from trauma or positioning
questions.explanation: Causes include edema, multiple attempts, oversized ETT, and excess movement.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old develops barky cough and stridor in PACU after extubation. What is the correct racemic epinephrine dose?
options: 2 mL of 0.5% epinephrine in 5 mL NS, nebulized
0.5 mL of 2.25% in 2.5 mL NS, nebulized
questions.explanation: Postextubation croup is treated with nebulized racemic epinephrine 0.5 mL of 2.25% in 2.5 mL NS.

questions.stem: A 15 kg child has postextubation croup. What dexamethasone dose range is appropriate?
options: 15–30 mg (1–2 mg/kg), given IV over 10 minutes
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone 0.1–0.5 mg/kg reduces airway edema; for 15 kg that is 1.5–7.5 mg.

questions.stem: Why is heliox used for croup?
options: Its low density reduces airflow resistance
It raises inspired oxygen content above 100%
questions.explanation: Helium lowers gas density and resistance.

questions.stem: Why is croup more severe in pediatric patients?
questions.explanation: Small airways increase resistance with edema.

questions.stem: Which airway-related injury generates the greatest number of anesthesia malpractice claims?
questions.explanation: Dental injury is the most common claim.

questions.stem: Which teeth are most often injured during laryngoscopy?
options: Mandibular molars on the right side
questions.explanation: Maxillary central incisors are most often affected.

questions.stem: After a difficult intubation, a patient has persistent hoarseness and a weak voice for weeks. Which laryngeal injuries could explain this? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Laryngeal trauma from intubation includes cord paralysis, granulomas, and arytenoid dislocation.

questions.stem: What signs suggest esophageal injury after difficult intubation?
options: Normal exam without symptoms in most cases
questions.explanation: Esophageal injury signs include neck edema, subcutaneous emphysema, and pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Why is esophageal perforation treated as a major emergency even if the initial airway problem is corrected?
options: The main consequence is transient dysphagia
questions.explanation: Mediastinitis has ~50% mortality.

questions.stem: Which factors increase tracheal injury risk? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Tracheal injury risk rises with overinflated cuffs, multiple attempts, large ETTs, stylets, steroids, and COPD.

questions.stem: Clinically significant pulmonary aspiration is uncommon. Which incidence best reflects the rate cited in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Clinically significant aspiration is ~1 in 35,000.

questions.stem: What are the two phases of aspiration pneumonitis?
questions.explanation: Phase 1 is chemical injury; phase 2 is inflammation.

questions.stem: What mask ventilation pressure limits reduce aspiration risk?
questions.explanation: Limit mask pressures to <15–20 cmH2O.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis is scheduled for GA. Which drugs reduce aspiration risk or harm? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Aspiration prophylaxis includes nonparticulate antacids, H2 blockers, PPIs, and prokinetics.

questions.stem: When is metoclopramide contraindicated?
options: Asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide is contraindicated in bowel obstruction and Parkinson's.

questions.stem: After intubation, chest movement and breath sounds appear reassuring but remain nonspecific. Which finding most reliably confirms tracheal placement?
questions.explanation: Capnography is most reliable.

questions.stem: Which are unreliable indicators of ETT placement? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Breath sounds, chest movement, fog, and epigastric auscultation are unreliable.

questions.stem: What additional sensitive method confirms tracheal placement?
options: Palpating the cuff in the neck
questions.explanation: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy is sensitive but not always practical.

questions.stem: Which complications follow esophageal intubation? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Complications include perforation, abscess, emphysema, pneumothorax, and mediastinitis.

questions.stem: A closed claims review of respiratory events finds one airway error stands out as a major contributor. Which is it?
questions.explanation: Unrecognized esophageal intubation is a significant contributor to respiratory closed claims.

questions.stem: During and after intubation, which complications should you watch for? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Intubation complications include airway trauma, aspiration, esophageal and endobronchial intubation, and ETT problems.

questions.stem: Which strategies prevent airway management complications? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Prevention includes careful technique, limited attempts, and cuff monitoring.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a full beard, BMI 38, OSA, Mallampati IV, TMD of 5 cm, and neck circumference 46 cm. Which techniques are predicted to be difficult? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Beard, obesity, and OSA predict difficult BMV; Mallampati IV and short TMD predict difficult laryngoscopy; obesity and thick neck complicate cric.

questions.stem: In that patient, what is the MOST appropriate preparation before induction?
options: Standard induction with a Mac 3 blade
Deep sedation without an airway backup plan
Plan a standard RSI with a Mac blade
Plan awake intubation or have VL, SGA, and FONA ready
questions.explanation: Multiple predictors call for a strategy that preserves spontaneous ventilation or a full backup setup.

questions.stem: A 70 kg patient is to receive 4% lidocaine topicalization. Using about 4.5 mg/kg as the max, what is the maximum dose?
How many mg are in 5 mL of 4% lidocaine?
A nebulizer uses 8 mL of 4% lidocaine. How many mg is that?
questions.explanation: 8 mL × 40 mg/mL = 320 mg.

questions.stem: A patient receives 8 mL of 4% lidocaine by nebulizer, then 2 mL of 2% for each SLN block (both sides). What is the total lidocaine?
A patient with an unstable cervical spine fracture needs intubation for surgery. Which technique is BEST?
options: Blind nasal intubation under deep sedation
Awake flexible scope intubation with topical anesthesia
Direct laryngoscopy with full neck extension
questions.explanation: Unstable C-spine is an indication for awake intubation that preserves spontaneous ventilation and allows a neuro check.

questions.stem: A patient with a large laryngeal tumor and stridor needs surgery. What is the BEST plan?
options: Awake intubation or surgical airway preparation
Rapid sequence induction with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: Airway tumors are indications for awake intubation and FONA readiness.

questions.stem: During induction, BMV is impossible despite OPA and two-hand seal. SpO2 is falling. What is the NEXT step?
options: Attempt intubation with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: Escalate to SGA when BMV fails.

questions.stem: After failed BMV and failed SGA, SpO2 is 70% and intubation fails. What is the NEXT step?
questions.explanation: CICO requires emergency front-of-neck access.

questions.stem: A CL grade III view is obtained with a Mac blade. What is the BEST next step?
options: Remove the blade and wake the patient immediately
Switch to a smaller blade without changes
Use a bougie or BURP, or switch to VL
questions.explanation: Poor views benefit from bougie, BURP, or VL.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy produces a Cormack-Lehane IIb view with only the posterior glottis visible. Which adjunct is most likely to facilitate tube placement?
questions.explanation: Bougies are used for IIb/III views.

questions.stem: During DL, the ETT will not pass over the bougie. What should be done?
options: Remove the bougie and push harder
Advance the bougie into the bronchus
questions.explanation: Rotate the ETT to free the bevel.

questions.stem: During VL with a hyperangulated blade, the view is excellent but the tube will not enter. What is MOST likely?
options: The glottis is not visible on the screen
The patient is in laryngospasm at the cords
The ETT is not shaped to follow the blade's angle
questions.explanation: Hyperangulated VL needs a rigid stylet or preshaped tube.

questions.stem: After VL intubation, the patient has blood in the oropharynx and a torn tonsillar pillar. What caused this?
options: Blind ETT advancement while looking at the screen
Excessive cuff pressure against the tonsillar pillar
questions.explanation: VL risks pharyngeal injury from indirect advancement.

questions.stem: A patient has limited mouth opening of 2 cm. Which technique is BEST?
questions.explanation: Restricted mouth opening favors flexible scope; LMA and DL are limited.

questions.stem: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis has fixed neck flexion. Which technique is MOST appropriate?
options: Flexible scope or VL rather than DL
DL with maximal extension of the neck
questions.explanation: Limited AO mobility makes DL difficult; FIS or VL are alternatives.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient at term needs GA for emergency cesarean. Which risk is highest?
questions.explanation: CICV incidence is about 1:300 in obstetrics.

questions.stem: A patient's cuff pressure reads 45 cmH2O during nitrous oxide use. What should be done?
options: Leave it, since N2O effects are temporary
Deflate the cuff and ventilate around it
Reduce the cuff pressure below 25 cmH2O
Increase the pressure to prevent aspiration
questions.explanation: Keep cuff pressure <25 cmH2O; N2O increases it.

questions.stem: A patient is intubated with an 8.5 mm ETT for a short case and later complains of sore throat and hoarseness. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Larger ETTs risk trauma, nerve injury, and sore throat.

questions.stem: A patient needs nasotracheal intubation for dental surgery. What preparation is required? (Select 3)
options: Grab the cuff with Magill forceps
questions.explanation: Prep includes nostril selection, vasoconstrictor, lubrication, bevel away from midline, and floor-of-nose passage.

questions.stem: During nasal intubation, the tube stops at 15 cm. What is the NEXT step?
options: Push harder through the resistance at 15 cm
Pull back and try the other nostril right away
Perform DL and guide the ETT with Magill forceps
questions.explanation: At 14–16 cm the tube is in the oropharynx; use DL and Magill forceps to guide it.

questions.stem: During nasal intubation, heavy epistaxis occurs. Which step could have reduced this?
options: Using a larger tube to tamponade bleeding
Advancing along the roof of the nose toward the turbinates
Vasoconstrictor and gentle insertion along the nasal floor
Using a larger ETT to tamponade the mucosa
questions.explanation: Vasoconstrictors and proper technique reduce bleeding.

questions.stem: During an awake FOI, the patient coughs and gags when the scope reaches the cords. Which block was likely omitted?
questions.explanation: The transtracheal block anesthetizes the cords and trachea.

questions.stem: During an awake oral FOI, the patient gags when the scope passes the tongue base. Which block would help?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal block anesthetizes the posterior tongue and oropharynx.

questions.stem: During an awake FOI, the patient coughs when the scope touches the epiglottis. Which block addresses this?
questions.explanation: The SLN block covers the supraglottic region including the epiglottis.

questions.stem: During awake intubation, the patient becomes apneic after a large dose of propofol. What principle was violated?
options: Use a long-acting opioid for comfort
Avoid deep sedation that can collapse the airway
Give deep sedation for comfort during scoping
questions.explanation: Deep sedation during awake intubation risks airway collapse.

questions.stem: Which sedative is often preferred for awake intubation because it preserves ventilation?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine provides sedation with minimal respiratory depression.

questions.stem: During awake FOI, secretions obscure the view. Which premedication would have helped?
questions.explanation: Antisialagogues like glycopyrrolate dry secretions.

questions.stem: During nebulized lidocaine topicalization, how long should you wait before attempting FOI?
questions.explanation: Nebulization requires 10–20 minutes.

questions.stem: A patient receives benzocaine spray and becomes cyanotic with SpO2 85% despite oxygen. What is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Benzocaine can cause methemoglobinemia.

questions.stem: During an SLN block, air is aspirated. What should you do?
options: Withdraw because the needle is in the pharynx
Inject, because air confirms the correct position
questions.explanation: Air means too deep (pharynx); withdraw and reposition.

questions.stem: During a transtracheal block, blood is aspirated. What should you do?
options: Reposition; blood means you are not in the trachea
Inject anyway at a slower rate to limit toxicity
questions.explanation: Air, not blood, confirms tracheal placement.

questions.stem: During the transtracheal block, the patient does not cough after injection. What is the MOST likely problem?
options: Lidocaine abolished the cough reflex before injection
The block worked perfectly and no cough is expected
The patient had too much sedation
Injection was not during inspiration or not in the trachea
questions.explanation: Coughing after inspiratory injection spreads anesthetic; absence suggests poor placement or timing.

questions.stem: Which cricoid pressure is appropriate after the patient loses consciousness per this lecture?
questions.explanation: This lecture lists 30–40 N after LOC.

questions.stem: During RSI with cricoid pressure, the view is poor. What is the BEST response?
options: Ease or release cricoid pressure to improve the view
Increase cricoid pressure to 60 N for better occlusion
Add BURP while keeping 60 N cricoid
questions.explanation: Cricoid pressure can impair visualization.

questions.stem: A trauma patient in a cervical collar cannot be intubated or ventilated, and you move to cricothyrotomy. What should you do with the collar?
options: Remove the front of the collar while an assistant holds inline stabilization
Leave the collar on at all costs
Perform the cric through the collar
Delay the cric until the collar can be replaced with a new one
questions.explanation: Neck impediments should be removed when possible, with manual inline stabilization maintained.

questions.stem: A patient has prior neck radiation and a large goiter. Which technique is MOST likely difficult?
questions.explanation: Radiation and tumor (SHORT) predict difficult cric.

questions.stem: In a patient with morbid obesity, cricothyroid landmarks cannot be palpated reliably. Which adjunct best helps identify the membrane before an emergency develops?
questions.explanation: POCUS helps locate the membrane in obese patients.

questions.stem: During TTJV, the chest does not fall between breaths. What is the risk?
options: Hypocarbia from overventilation through the catheter
questions.explanation: Incomplete exhalation causes air trapping and barotrauma.

questions.stem: During TTJV, which settings are recommended? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: TTJV uses a low rate of 8–10/min and an I:E of 1:3 to 1:4 so trapped gas can escape through the upper airway.

questions.stem: During TTJV, the patient develops neck swelling and crepitus. What complication is this?
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema is a TTJV complication.

questions.stem: A retrograde wire is passed and retrieved from the mouth. What should be done at the neck?
options: Cut the wire flush with skin
Clamp the wire to prevent migration
Remove the wire immediately after retrieval
questions.explanation: Clamp the wire at the neck, then railroad the ETT.

questions.stem: During retrograde intubation, when is the wire removed?
options: When resistance is met during ETT advancement
Before advancing the ETT into the pharynx
questions.explanation: Remove the wire at the neck once resistance is met, then advance the ETT further.

questions.stem: A trauma patient will require prolonged mechanical ventilation. Which definitive airway is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Long-term ventilation is a tracheotomy indication.

questions.stem: During tracheotomy, which injury risk is highlighted?
questions.explanation: Major vascular injury includes the innominate artery.

questions.stem: A healthy patient for a 30-minute knee arthroscopy with an empty stomach. Which airway is MOST appropriate?
options: LMA as an alternative to an ETT
questions.explanation: SGAs are an alternative to ETTs for elective surgery.

questions.stem: If an SGA is chosen for laparoscopic cholecystectomy, which design feature is most desirable?
questions.explanation: ProSeal is used in laparoscopic cases with higher seal and gastric drainage.

questions.stem: A patient in active labor needs GA for emergency cesarean. Why avoid an SGA as the primary airway?
options: SGAs are avoided in obstetric patients due to aspiration risk
SGAs cause more airway trauma in pregnancy
SGAs cause hypertension in pregnant patients
SGAs require neuromuscular blockade in pregnancy
questions.explanation: The lecture advises avoiding SGAs in obstetric patients.

questions.stem: A patient with subglottic stenosis needs ventilation. Why is an SGA not effective?
options: SGAs cause laryngospasm when stenosis is present
SGAs are too small to seal adult subglottic airways
SGAs require awake placement in all stenosis cases
questions.explanation: SGAs are ineffective with airway pathology below the glottis.

questions.stem: An LMA is placed and the cuff pressure is 80 cmH2O. What is the risk?
options: Lower airway resistance from a wider seal
Opening the upper esophageal sphincter and gastric insufflation
An improved seal with a lower aspiration risk overall
questions.explanation: Overinflation >60 cmH2O can open the esophagus.

questions.stem: An LMA is placed and ventilation is poor with high peak pressures. What is a likely cause?
options: Cuff underinflation, with a normal position
Malposition folding the epiglottis over the glottis
Excellent seal with no leak at peak pressure
Low airway resistance from a wide lumen
questions.explanation: Malposition can obstruct the airway by displacing the epiglottis.

questions.stem: An LMA is used for rescue in a CICV patient. What is the advantage?
options: Fast, easy insertion with high rescue success
It protects against aspiration during rescue
It allows controlled ventilation at high pressures
questions.explanation: SGAs are fast, easy rescue tools with high success.

questions.stem: The team wants an SGA that can serve as a conduit for tracheal intubation. Which type best supports that plan?
options: Classic LMA without an intubation conduit
Intubating SGA such as Fastrach or AuraGain
questions.explanation: Some SGAs are designed as intubation conduits.

questions.stem: A patient's LMA leaks at 12 cmH2O despite repositioning. What does this suggest?
options: Normal leak pressure for all SGA designs
The patient is ready for extubation and PACU
Difficult SGA ventilation; consider alternative airway
Adequate seal for all ventilation needs
questions.explanation: Leaks <15 cmH2O suggest difficulty.

questions.stem: A patient with airway edema and difficult intubation is ready for extubation. Which strategy is BEST?
options: Extubate over an airway exchange catheter
Extubate deep without a backup device
questions.explanation: AECs allow reversible extubation and guided reintubation.

questions.stem: After extubation over an AEC, the patient develops stridor. What is the BEST next step?
options: Reintubate over the AEC with laryngoscope assistance
Remove the AEC and give racemic epinephrine
Advance the AEC into the bronchus
questions.explanation: The AEC guides reintubation.

questions.stem: When reintubating over an AEC, the ETT meets resistance at the glottis. What should you do?
options: Push harder through the resistance at the glottis
Remove the AEC and try blind
Slightly retract and rotate the ETT 90° counterclockwise
questions.explanation: Retract slightly and rotate 90° counterclockwise.

questions.stem: A patient remains intubated after head and neck surgery with significant edema. Which decision is MOST appropriate?
options: Extubate in the OR with a steroid dose
Extubate without a cuff leak test
Extubate deep to avoid coughing on the tube
questions.explanation: Delayed extubation is an option for high-risk patients.

questions.stem: A patient has no cuff leak after prone spine surgery with large fluid volumes. What does this suggest?
options: Laryngotracheal edema and high extubation risk
Safe extubation conditions after prone surgery
questions.explanation: Lack of cuff leak suggests edema.

questions.stem: A patient at the end of surgery has TOFR 0.7, VC 10 mL/kg, and weak grip. Should the patient be extubated?
options: No; NM strength and VC do not meet criteria
Yes; TOFR above 0.5 is sufficient for extubation
Yes; VC over 5 mL/kg is sufficient
Yes; hand grip is not required
questions.explanation: Criteria require TOFR >0.9 and VC >15 mL/kg.

questions.stem: A patient has TOFR 0.95, VC 18 mL/kg, NIF −30 cmH2O, SpO2 96% on FiO2 0.4. Are respiratory criteria met?
options: No, NIF must be more negative than −60 cmH2O
questions.explanation: These values meet the lecture criteria.

questions.stem: A patient has a head lift of 2 seconds and weak grip. What does this suggest?
options: Adequate strength for immediate extubation now
questions.explanation: Criteria require head lift >5 seconds and strong grip.

questions.stem: A patient is in stage II during emergence and coughing. What is the BEST action?
options: Avoid extubation until deeper or fully awake
Extubate now, since coughing shows reflexes are intact
questions.explanation: Avoid extubating during stage II.

questions.stem: A patient is extubated and develops complete laryngospasm with SpO2 80%. After Larson maneuver and positive pressure fail, what is next?
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine is given if desaturation persists.

questions.stem: After laryngospasm resolves, the patient has pink frothy sputum. What is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: NPPE follows forceful inspiration against a closed glottis.

questions.stem: Which technique reduces laryngospasm risk at extubation?
options: Suction while the patient is light
Stimulate the airway to trigger waking
Extubate deep in stage III or fully awake
questions.explanation: Avoid airway irritation during light anesthesia.

questions.stem: A child is extubated after multiple intubation attempts and develops stridor 2 hours later. What is MOST likely?
options: Laryngospasm from secretions on the vocal cords
questions.explanation: Croup occurs within 3 hours, especially after multiple attempts.

questions.stem: A child develops postextubation stridor consistent with croup but is still moving air adequately. Which initial treatment is most appropriate?
options: Immediate reintubation with a larger tube
questions.explanation: Treatment includes humidified O2, racemic epinephrine, dexamethasone, and heliox.

questions.stem: A 20 kg child with croup is given dexamethasone. What is the dose range?
A patient with residual NMB is extubated and develops upper airway obstruction. What is the BEST treatment?
options: Give flumazenil to reverse residual weakness
Remove oxygen to stimulate the respiratory drive
Support ventilation and reverse with sugammadex if appropriate
Give additional rocuronium to relax the airway
questions.explanation: Residual NMB requires reversal and support.

questions.stem: A patient reports a chipped maxillary incisor after intubation. What do closed claims data say about this complication?
options: Dental injury involves molars more than incisors
Dental injury is the most common anesthesia malpractice claim
Dental injury is rare and seldom documented
Dental injury occurs mainly with videolaryngoscopy
questions.explanation: Dental injury is the most common anesthesia claim, most often involving the maxillary incisors.

questions.stem: A patient has persistent hoarseness after prolonged intubation with a large ETT. What complication is likely?
questions.explanation: Prolonged intubation and large ETTs can cause granulomas.

questions.stem: After difficult intubation, a patient develops neck swelling, subcutaneous air, and fever. What is MOST concerning?
options: Laryngospasm from secretions after extubation in PACU
questions.explanation: Esophageal injury can lead to mediastinitis.

questions.stem: After intubation, breath sounds are heard bilaterally but ETCO2 is absent. What is the BEST interpretation?
options: Correct tracheal placement confirmed by sounds
questions.explanation: Breath sounds are unreliable; capnography is most reliable.

questions.stem: After intubation, the tube is fogging but ETCO2 is absent. What should be done?
questions.explanation: Condensation is unreliable; absent ETCO2 suggests esophageal placement.

questions.stem: A patient has a history of GERD and full stomach. Which mask ventilation pressure should be used?
options: As high as needed to see chest rise
questions.explanation: Limit mask pressures to reduce aspiration.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson's disease needs aspiration prophylaxis. Which drug should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide is contraindicated in Parkinson's.

questions.stem: A patient aspirates during induction. What happens in phase 1 of aspiration pneumonitis?
questions.explanation: Phase 1 is direct chemical injury; phase 2 is inflammation.

questions.stem: A patient is intubated in the ICU. How much more likely is death or brain damage from airway events in the ICU than the OR?
questions.explanation: Adverse airway events are 30–60× more likely in ED/ICU.

questions.stem: A patient with epiglottitis needs an airway. Which technique should be avoided?
options: Controlled inhalation induction with surgical backup
questions.explanation: FIS should be avoided in epiglottitis.

questions.stem: A patient with airway burns needs intubation. Which tool is not recommended?
questions.explanation: FIS is avoided in airway burns per the lecture.

questions.stem: A patient has severe airway bleeding and needs intubation. What is the main limitation of VL?
options: Blood can obscure the camera view
VL cannot be used with an LMA in place
questions.explanation: Blood and secretions can obscure the VL view.

questions.stem: A patient needs intubation during CICO with no time for FOI. Why is FIS not ideal?
options: It is slow and not suited for emergent CICO
It is the fastest emergency method available
questions.explanation: FIS is not ideal for emergent CICO.

questions.stem: A patient has a failed intubation but can be ventilated with an LMA. Which next step is appropriate?
options: Intubate through the SGA with a flexible scope
questions.explanation: FIS through an SGA is an option when ventilation is possible.

questions.stem: A patient has an anticipated difficult airway and a cooperative mental status. Which approach is BEST?
options: Rapid sequence induction with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: Awake intubation preserves spontaneous ventilation.

questions.stem: During an awake fiberoptic intubation, the patient becomes combative and SpO2 drops to 82%. What does this situation illustrate?
options: It requires deep sedation to succeed
Flexible scopes prevent hypoxia during scoping
Flexible scopes work best in uncooperative, hypoxic patients
questions.explanation: Flexible scope intubation is avoided in uncooperative or severely hypoxic patients because it takes time and cooperation.

questions.stem: A patient's MMC is class II, TMD 7 cm, interincisor gap 4 cm, and neck mobility is normal. What is the expected difficulty?
questions.explanation: Normal findings predict low difficulty, though no test is perfect.

questions.stem: A patient has TMD 10 cm. What is the concern?
options: Caudally placed larynx with deep visual field
Anterior larynx that is hard to bring into view
questions.explanation: TMD >9 cm suggests a caudal larynx.

questions.stem: A patient has a 1-fingerbreadth hyoid-to-thyroid distance. What is the concern?
questions.explanation: Less than 2 fingerbreadths suggests an anterior larynx.

questions.stem: A patient cannot touch chin to chest or extend the neck. What does this suggest?
options: Low Mallampati class with an easy view
Easy mask ventilation with normal anatomy
Limited range of motion predicting difficult laryngoscopy
Normal range of motion for the patient's age and size
questions.explanation: Limited head and neck ROM is a difficulty predictor.

questions.stem: A patient has a highly arched palate. What does this predict?
options: Easy intubation with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: A highly arched or narrow palate suggests difficulty.

questions.stem: A patient is edentulous. How does this affect BMV?
questions.explanation: Edentulous patients have altered facial structure and poor seal.

questions.stem: An elderly patient with well-fitting dentures has a poor mask seal once the dentures are removed. What is the BEST approach?
options: Remove the dentures before mask ventilation
Use a smaller mask so it sits inside the sunken cheeks
Use a smaller mask without dentures
Leave the dentures in for BMV
questions.explanation: Dentures can be left in during BMV if they improve the seal, then removed before laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient has an NG tube and mask seal is poor. What is an option?
options: Give lidocaine to relax the cords
questions.explanation: NG tube removal may improve the seal.

questions.stem: A patient has a CL grade I view. What does this predict?
questions.explanation: Grades I–IIa are generally easier.

questions.stem: On DL, you cannot see the epiglottis or any glottic structure. What is the BEST next step?
options: Switch to VL or readjust your technique
Change to a smaller blade and repeat the same attempt
questions.explanation: With a grade IV view, readjust positioning or technique, or move to videolaryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient's Mallampati is class III and TMD is 5 cm. What is the combined implication?
options: Low risk of difficulty with these findings
BMV is difficult but laryngoscopy is not
Mask ventilation is affected but laryngoscopy is not
questions.explanation: Combining predictors increases accuracy.

questions.stem: A patient has a long upper incisor overbite. What does the exam table suggest?
options: Mask seal is affected but laryngoscopy is not
Easier laryngoscopy from a wider view
questions.explanation: Prominent overbite suggests difficulty.

questions.stem: A patient's ULBT is class B. What does this mean?
options: Normal Mallampati with class I view
Lower incisors align but bite below the vermilion border
Lower incisors bite above the vermilion border
questions.explanation: Class B aligns with upper incisors but bites below the vermilion border.

questions.stem: A patient's SMD is 11 cm. What does this suggest?
options: Normal airway with low predicted difficulty
questions.explanation: SMD <12.5 cm is associated with difficulty.

questions.stem: A patient's atlantooccipital extension is 18°. What does this predict?
questions.explanation: Extension <23° predicts difficulty.

questions.stem: A patient's neck circumference is 48 cm. Which risk increases?
questions.explanation: Neck circumference >43 cm suggests difficulty.

questions.stem: A patient has a 2.5-cm mouth opening. Which three airway maneuvers or devices are directly limited by the restricted oral aperture? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Restricted opening limits blades, SGAs, and ETTs; nasal FIS may work.

questions.stem: A patient with Down syndrome presents for anesthesia. Which paired airway concern is most important to anticipate?
options: Airway obstruction with limited cervical mobility
Increased mouth opening with easier laryngoscopy
Reduced tongue size with improved mask ventilation
questions.explanation: Down syndrome is associated with airway obstruction and cervical issues.

questions.stem: A patient with Pierre Robin sequence needs anesthesia. What airway risk is expected?
questions.explanation: Pierre Robin is a congenital cause of obstruction.

questions.stem: A patient has severe hypotension and acidosis before intubation. Which difficult airway category applies?
questions.explanation: Severe hypoxia, hypotension, or acidosis create a physiologic difficult airway.

questions.stem: A patient has a large neck hematoma after carotid surgery. What difficulty category applies?
questions.explanation: Hematomas are pathophysiologic causes.

questions.stem: A patient has facial trauma and cannot open the mouth. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Prepare for surgical airway or cricothyrotomy
Standard DL with a Mac 4 blade and stylet
questions.explanation: Traumatic facial injury may require front-of-neck access.

questions.stem: A patient's airway plan includes backup devices and FONA readiness. Which algorithm concept does this reflect?
options: Avoiding backup plans to save induction time
Planning for primary and alternative strategies
questions.explanation: Algorithms emphasize primary and backup plans.

questions.stem: A patient's airway plan is based on the Airway Approach Algorithm. Which question addresses aspiration?
options: Is the patient at risk of rapid desaturation?
questions.explanation: One question asks whether aspiration risk has been minimized.

questions.stem: A patient's airway plan includes apneic oxygenation. Which patient benefits MOST?
options: A healthy patient with normal FRC
questions.explanation: Obese patients desaturate quickly and benefit most.

questions.stem: A patient's preoxygenation is limited by a poor mask seal. What is the MOST appropriate adjunct?
options: Apneic oxygenation with high-flow nasal cannula
Lower FiO2 to reduce absorption atelectasis
Vital capacity breaths through the same mask
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation can help maintain oxygenation during intubation.

questions.stem: A patient's airway is secured, and the ETT is at 28 cm at the lip in a 5'2" woman. What is a concern?
questions.explanation: Deep insertion risks mainstem intubation, usually right.

questions.stem: A patient is intubated with a 6.0 ETT and has high airway resistance. What is the likely cause?
options: Resistance stays about the same across tube sizes
questions.explanation: Smaller ETTs increase resistance and work of breathing.

questions.stem: A patient's ETT cuff pressure is 10 cmH2O and there is a leak. What should be done?
options: Leave the leak, since cuff pressure should stay near zero
Increase to the minimum pressure that stops the leak, under 25 cmH2O
Deflate the cuff and ventilate around it
Increase to 40 cmH2O for a tight seal
questions.explanation: Inflate to the minimum volume that prevents leaks, <25 cmH2O.

questions.stem: A patient's airway plan includes marking the cricothyroid membrane. Which patients benefit? (Select 3)
options: Patients with Mallampati I and normal neck
questions.explanation: Mark the membrane in high-risk patients.

questions.stem: A CRNA confirms tracheal placement after intubation. What is the MOST reliable single method?
questions.explanation: ETCO2 capnography is most reliable.

questions.stem: During direct laryngoscopy, the epiglottis and posterior arytenoid structures are visible, but the vocal cords are not. Which view and next maneuver BEST fit?
options: Grade IV; proceed to cric immediately
Grade IIb–III range; use a bougie or BURP
Grade I; pass the tube directly under vision
questions.explanation: Seeing only posterior structures is a poor view; bougie or BURP helps.

questions.stem: During a preoperative airway exam, only the hard palate is visible with maximal mouth opening and tongue protrusion. Which Mallampati class is present?
questions.explanation: Class IV shows hard palate only.

questions.stem: Which head-and-neck position BEST aligns the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes for direct laryngoscopy?
options: Head elevated on a pad with head extension (sniffing)
Head flat on the bed in a neutral position
Head elevated on a pad without extension
Head rotated to the side with the neck flexed
questions.explanation: Sniffing position aligns the axes.

questions.stem: After a curved laryngoscope blade is inserted along the right side of the mouth, what should occur NEXT?
options: Lift straight up without moving the tongue aside
Rock the blade back on the upper teeth for leverage
Rotate the handle clockwise toward the teeth
Sweep the tongue left and advance to the midline tongue base
questions.explanation: Insert right, sweep tongue left, advance midline, then lift forward at 45°.

questions.stem: During nasal intubation, the tube should be advanced along the nasal floor beneath which structure to reduce mucosal trauma?
questions.explanation: The tube follows the nasal floor beneath the inferior turbinate.

questions.stem: A lesion is centered in the pharyngeal segment at approximately C5–C6. Which segment is involved?
questions.explanation: The hypopharynx is at C5–C6.

questions.stem: After thyroid surgery, a patient develops new hoarseness and an ineffective cough. Which nerve was MOST likely injured?
questions.explanation: RLN injury causes hoarseness.

questions.stem: Emergency front-of-neck access is required after failed oxygenation. Which structure is the key surface landmark for cricothyrotomy?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane lies between thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

questions.stem: After intubation of a small adult, the ETT is secured at 26 cm and breath sounds are absent on the left. What is MOST likely?
options: Left mainstem intubation from a deep tube
questions.explanation: The steeper right bronchus favors right mainstem intubation.

questions.stem: Refer to the 3-3-2 summary. A patient has 2 fingerbreadths of mouth opening. What does this predict?
options: Anterior larynx that is hard to visualize
questions.explanation: Fewer than 3 fingerbreadths suggests inadequate opening.

questions.stem: Refer to the difficult airway cart figure. Which item confirms tube position?
questions.explanation: Confirmation tools include capnography and esophageal detectors.

questions.stem: Refer to the awake intubation medication table. Which agent is both a topical anesthetic and vasoconstrictor?
questions.explanation: Cocaine provides topical anesthesia and vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: Refer to the airway block nerve figure. Which nerve provides sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve supplies the anterior tongue.

questions.stem: During a glossopharyngeal nerve block near the tonsillar pillar, why is aspiration before injection essential?
options: It confirms nerve stimulation before injecting
The carotid artery lies close to the injection site
It confirms tracheal placement of the needle
It prevents coughing during the injection
questions.explanation: Avoid intravascular injection near the carotid.

questions.stem: During a superior laryngeal nerve block, what tactile finding suggests the needle has passed through the thyrohyoid membrane?
options: A loss of resistance to air in a syringe
questions.explanation: Resistance or a bounce indicates the thyrohyoid membrane.

questions.stem: Refer to the cricoid pressure figure. What structure is occluded against the vertebrae?
questions.explanation: Cricoid pressure compresses the esophagus against the cervical spine.

questions.stem: Refer to the extubation risk factors table. Which surgical factor increases difficult extubation risk?
questions.explanation: Head and neck surgery increases difficult extubation risk.

questions.stem: Refer to the airway trauma figure. Which complication is associated with arytenoid dislocation?
questions.explanation: Laryngeal trauma causes hoarseness and possible obstruction.

questions.stem: Refer to the figure on confirming ETT placement. Which confirmation method is highly sensitive but not always practical?
questions.explanation: Seeing tracheal rings with a bronchoscope is sensitive but not always available or practical; capnography is the standard.
